text:
11 weeks ago I published the architecture of this exact move. Today he executed it on camera. Let me walk you through what you just watched, slowly.

10:20 this morning: David Sacks tells Anthropic and OpenAI to "stop pretending you need anyone else's permission" to slow down AI development.

12:29 this afternoon: Dario Amodei announces he'd be willing to hand Anthropic over to "the right combination of governments."

Two hours. The political cover for "we're being responsible" got ripped off at breakfast, and by lunch the merger stopped being a classified rumor and became an on-camera offer. That's not a coincidence. That's a system that no longer thinks it needs to hide.

Understand what "willing to hand over" actually is. It's not generosity. It's the last exit. Anthropic bleeds $21 billion a year on $13 billion of revenue. The IPO window is shut. Stargate's $500 billion went to OpenAI. That $965 billion valuation exists on exactly one condition: nobody is allowed to compete. The gate stopped being ideology a long time ago. It is the revenue strategy.

And here's the part that should make you furious.

The last time "national security" justified this machine - the Mythos breach, the global export bans, the trusted-partner tiers - the NSA's 340 vulnerabilities stayed open. They signed a Risk Acceptance Memo. The tile turned green. The holes are still there today, in the same configurations, on the same boxes. The company that found them is embedded inside the agency that didn't fix them, and now it is offering to be owned by the governments that papered it over.

If security were the point, the patching would have been the point.

Meanwhile the tide keeps rising. DeepSeek V4 Pro is MIT-licensed at $0.87 per million tokens. Open weights are one generation behind and closing. This very morning the internet was passing around a "pirate bay for models" built by one guy with a Render account. You cannot ban weights. Everyone knows it now.

So if you can't gate the technology, you gate the institution. You become the government's AI before open models make "the government's AI" meaningless. It's the last movable piece on the board, and he moved it at 12:29 on a Sunday afternoon.

"The right combination of governments" is not a sentence about safety. It's a price tag wearing a principle. He is shopping for a landlord - and the landlords-in-waiting, Amazon, Google, Singapore's sovereign fund, Qatar, already own chunks of the building.

I wrote in June that the velvet rope was never about safety. It was about who holds the keys when the money runs out.

Today the money answered. And it's asking for your government as the down payment.

text:
Imagine you’re a conman. You’ve said for years you have MAGIC BEANS. You’ve shown lots of REALLY BIG normal beans that you made in your lab. 

“Almost there!” you say—over and over.

Now, you have *almost* convinced the villagers to give you TWO TRILLION DOLLARS.

But while the beans keep getting bigger. No magic yet…

What do you do? That money is SO CLOSE.

“I know!” you think, “instead of MAGIC beans, lets’s make them KILLER BEANS.”

So you pump up your beans up SUPER BIG and you say: “I’m sorry, but these BEANS ARE GETTING BIGGER ON THEIR OWN!” You threaten people that if they don’t give you the money, the beans may get into the WRONG HANDS. They might get BIGGER THAN THE EARTH!

The villagers, aghast, run to and fro arguing whether the beans are going to kill everyone or make them all rich.

“Well, either way,” the idiots in the village conclude, “We’d better give him the money.”

quoted_text:
Zuckerberg lays out Meta’s product strategy for personal agents pretty clearly in this interview w/ @alexeheath @finkd. Would hate to compete with him - super capable and focused.

>Distribution + subsidy: billions of existing users, hundreds of millions of small businesses, and cash flows to fund up to 100M free tokens/week plus a virtual computer. Expensive for independent agent companies to compete with.

>Personal context + protection: connect social w/ email, messages, health and business tools, with limited permissions, secure credentials and sentinel agents checking activity. A confidential VM is being developed so even Meta can’t see its contents.

>Specific, recurring tasks: order ingredients, secure permits, review training footage, build software and manage ads. Remember what worked, suggest improvements and eventually interact with other people’s agents.

>Models built for those jobs: coding to execute tasks and discretion to use personal information without unnecessarily sharing it. He describes Watermelon as a significantly more advanced, larger pre-train than Avocado, with further post-training gains to come.

>Compute already supporting the next generation: Zuckerberg says the gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster in Ohio is online and training models beyond Watermelon. He doesn’t specify how much of that capacity is energized or utilized.

>Monetization through subscriptions and small transaction fees, potentially paid by businesses. The aim is for agents to make or save users enough money to support the service.

Meta is spending to own the models and infrastructure while using its existing business to fund distribution. Zuckerberg is unusually explicit here about the products and economics he wants that investment to enable.

text:
David Sacks对今天Dario的限速论的评价值得一看，简单总结几条供大家参考：

1.OpenAI和 Anthropic本身就是前沿AI的主导者，如果真认为风险太高，完全可以自行减速，不需要等政府或同行批准。

2.Dario和Sam不应把“限速”包装成必须全行业协调的公共安全方案，否则容易演变成借安全之名推动一套行业统一规则，这套规则最终可能巩固OpenAI和Anthropic现有的领先地位。

3.他反对以反垄断豁免、特殊监管审批和统一第三方评估体系作为限速的前提，认为这可能压制并不处于前沿的竞争者。
4.他质疑METR等评估机构的独立性，认为其与Anthropic的投资者和员工存在过深联系。

5.OpenAI和Anthropic推动限速并不完全是利他主义，也有降低网络安全事故、产品责任和商业风险的现实利益。

6.提高模型可靠性、可预测性并减少越权行为，本身也是客户需求，因此“对齐”的同时也是正常的产品优化。

7. 中国大概率不会参加全球AI限速协议，因此任何美国监管或减速方案都必须考虑中美竞争现实。

8.如果OpenAI和Anthropic真的主动减速，会获得政治和社会信誉；如果拒绝自行行动却坚持要求监管配套，就会让人怀疑这是监管俘获或政治操作。

text:
最近有很多关于 RSI（Recursive Self-Improvement，递归自我改进）的讨论，也让大家开始担心，AI 会不会不断升级自己，最后超出人的控制

我周末集中看了一批 RSI 2026 年的论文和公开项目，想把几个问题讲清楚：现在到底发展到了哪一步，业界 popular 的讨论是什么，以及我们普通人能怎么用。最后我会给大家一个可以用来直接给 AI 实现初步 RSI 的 Prompt

这次按方向来聊，论文和项目放在对应段落，大家可以收藏下来慢慢看

1/ 先分清楚，大家说的“自我改进”，有三件不同的事
第一件，AI 根据反馈，把当前任务再做一遍。

第二件，它把有效经验、工具或工作流程留下来，下一次任务也能用上。

第三件，它进一步改进“下一轮怎么学习、怎么做实验、怎么选方案”这套方法。

越往后，接手的研发决策越多。9 月 10 日发表的的《The Last AI Built by Humans》把这些自主范围拆成了执行、策略、经验获取、环境适应和元改进几层，适合当阅读地图 https://t.co/aOWmBcFure

2/ 今年一条很密集方向研究线，是让 AI 改自己的 Harness

Harness 可以理解为模型周围那套实际干活的系统：读哪些文件、给模型看什么上下文、怎么调用工具、失败后怎么恢复、什么时候算完成。

今年 3 月的 Meta-Harness，6 月首发、8 月更新的 Self-Harness，以及 7 月底的 DarwinX （Salesforce），都在研究怎样把这套系统交给自动实验来优化

3/ 另一条已经出现企业内部应用的路线，是把人的纠错变成持久经验

今年 1 月的 MemRL，把经验和“这条经验实际有多管用”一起保存。下次先找相关经验，再根据使用效果挑选，而不只是找文字最相似的记录
https://t.co/kJ8zPuFy4G

到了 9 月 2 日，Meta 公开了一个更贴近日常工作的内部案例：专家纠正 Agent 后，系统会判断错误来自知识缺口还是处理流程，把纠错转成文件修改，重放原来的问题、跑回归测试，再交专家审核。

text:
大开眼界。

有人把 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 的 Causal Encoder-Decoder 思路，移植到了现有的 Qwen3-8B 上。

结果相当夸张。

不修改 Qwen3-8B 本身，只在模型外面增加一个负责近似后半层 KV 的小模型，Prefill 时间就缩短了接近一半，最终输出保持一致。

这件事对我们在 DGX Spark 上部署本地模型的意义很大。

本地模型现在最折磨人的地方，经常不是逐字生成有多慢，而是第一次加载长上下文时，要等很久才能吐出第一个 token。

系统提示词、Skills、工具定义、项目代码、历史对话和检索文档一起塞进去以后，模型需要先让整段输入经过所有 Transformer 层，为每一层计算 KV Cache。

这一步就是 Prefill。

上下文越长，Prefill 越重。到了几十万 token，哪怕后面生成速度还能接受，前面那段等待也足以让本地 Agent 用起来很难受。

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 的新结构，把模型拆成前后二十层。

前半部分像 Causal Encoder，负责处理输入。后半部分在生成阶段继续承担完整推理，但输入阶段使用由 Encoder 最终状态投影出来的共享 KV，不再让长提示词完整跑遍所有后半层。

官方模型因此只在 Prefill 阶段激活约 8B 参数，生成阶段激活约 16B。它还进一步压缩并复用 KV Cache，把全局 KV 压到大约每 token 890 字节。

原本我以为这种收益必须重新训练整套模型才能获得。

这次实验真正让我大开眼界的地方，在于研究者直接对现有 Qwen3-8B 做了近似。

模型权重不用改。

只要额外训练一个近似模块，让它根据前面得到的状态预测后半层需要的 KV，就有机会跳过一部分重复计算。

如果这个方法能在更多模型和任务上稳定复现，未来 DGX Spark 上的本地部署可能会进步得非常疯狂。

我们不一定要等下一代模型发布。

Llama、Qwen、DeepSeek 蒸馏模型，以及各种已经完成微调的垂直模型，都可能通过外挂近似模型获得一次推理升级。原来的模型继续负责生成，新增的小模型负责压缩 Prefill 成本。

这种优化非常适合本地 Agent。

Coding Agent 每次都要读取大量项目文件。Computer Use Agent 会反复携带操作历史和界面状态。Deep Research 会装入长文档。多 Agent 系统还会重复发送工具定义、记忆和任务背景。

这些工作负载都在不断支付 Prefill 成本。

如果 Prefill 真能普遍缩短一半，我们在 Spark 上打开大型代码库、加载十几万 token 的上下文、运行长时间 Agent 时，首 token 等待会明显下降。同一台机器也能更快处理并发任务。

更令人期待的是 KV Cache。

DGX Spark 有 128GB 统一内存，能让许多大型量化模型跑起来，但长上下文和多个并发 Agent 会迅速吃掉 KV Cache。模型权重勉强装下，不代表它还能给多个会话留下足够的上下文空间。

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 已经证明，Transformer 不需要永远为每一层保存一套完整 KV。后半层状态可以投影，可以共享，也可以近似。只要近似误差受到控制，过去被认为必须保存的东西，可能有很大一部分都能省掉。

对 Spark 这种内存容量很大、带宽却远低于顶级数据中心 GPU 的设备来说，这类架构优化可能比单纯增加算力更有价值。

少读一半权重，少搬一大块 KV，减少长提示词经过的层数，带来的不只是跑分快一点。它可能直接改变哪些模型能够在单机上实用。

当然，现在还不能把这次结果理解成 Qwen3-8B 已经全面提速两倍。

作者展示的是 Prefill 时间减半，不是生成速度翻倍。测试规模、上下文长度、任务覆盖和输出一致性的评价方式也需要进一步公开。近似模块能否在代码、数学、长文本检索和工具调用中都保持可靠，还要看更完整的实验。

它也不能让 552B 参数的 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 突然塞进一台 DGX Spark。模型权重、Engram 参数和推理框架仍然有很高的部署门槛。

可这次实验已经展示了一个非常诱人的方向。

本地模型优化以后可能不只靠量化、剪枝、推测解码和更快的推理引擎。我们还可以给已有模型增加一个轻量近似层，重新安排它处理输入和生成时使用的计算量。

模型训练完，并不代表它的架构红利已经全部用完。

未来我们在 Spark 上部署同一个模型，可能今天还要等十秒读取上下文，几个月后换一个推理框架，再外挂一个近似 Encoder，时间就只剩五秒。继续叠加 KV 量化、缓存持久化和推测解码以后，整套 Agent 的体感可能完全不同。

硬件没有换。

模型权重也没有换。

真正疯狂进步的，可能是我们终于学会了怎样少算一点，同时尽量不损失模型原本的能力。

text:
For a decade, @a16z's MO was to funnel huge amounts of capital into scalable software companies to fund fragile growth and produce spurious markups.  

They now pretend they've always known that doesn't work, talking about coordination issues and overheads linked to raising too much. 

Then they claim it actually does work with AI because you can keep throwing money at compute and it will just magically build great products. 

This is such transparent nonsense. 

The coordinated misrepresentation of the venture market from this firm is beginning to feel desperate. 

The core claim: "Right now, clearly the power law is more extreme than it has been in the last 10 to 20 years of technology investing." - @DavidGeorge83 

What this read misses is that the winners may be larger, but they've also absorbed much more capital. 

"Power law" describes the long right tail of extreme outcomes. Essentially, how the vast majority of VC investments return <1x, while some return >100x or even >1000x. Across a portfolio the math works. 

So, has the power law become more or less extreme as venture capital has been increasingly dominated by giant fee-printing machines like @a16z?

On a dollar-weighted basis, the power law has probably flattened significantly as large outcomes have absorbed so much more capital — compressing the resulting multiples.

We can, for example, split the markets into all venture-backed companies versus a pool of companies that raised a Series D round or beyond. 

The logic is pretty clear. If you drive more money into venture capital, you systematically reduce the quality of outlier returns; fewer companies lose money, at the cost of fewer large outcomes.

Scaled venture platforms that are pumping capital into ever larger and later rounds have eroded the power law nature of venture capital.

quoted_text:
a16z's David George says AI's power law is becoming more extreme because dollars alone can compound a company's advantage:

"Right now, clearly the power law is more extreme than it has been in the last 10 to 20 years of technology investing, probably going back to the emergence of the network effect-driven consumer companies."

"Increasing returns to scale have always been a dynamic in our business... Brand reputation in the market, the accumulation of resources, all provide competitive advantages."

"That all still is the case. But right now, especially with the labs, for the first time in my career, you can take capital and throw it at a company, and it compounds their advantage."

"How do you screw up a startup? Throw too much money at it and have them hire 1,000 people, and then you create all these coordination issues and overhead issues and dueling priorities... because you can't hire enough people to do enough things fast enough."

As of Friday, Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has officially been shut down after recent attacks, putting -4 million barrels of daily oil exports at risk.

Meanwhile, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is now at risk of being shut down, threatening up to -9 million barrels of daily oil supply.

All while the Strait of Hormuz is operating at ~20% of its pre-Iran War capacity, removing -15 million barrels of daily oil flows.

Combined, this represents nearly ~30 MILLION barrels per day of oil flows that are either offline or at risk.

Even after accounting for some overlap between these routes, the scale of the potential disruption is enormous relative to the ~100 million barrel per day global oil market.

This is one of the most severe energy supply situations in modern history.

text:
In the early 19th century in France, there were these group called the Saint-Simonians. They were followers of this chap named Henri de Saint-Simon who believed that organised industry would overcome poverty and social conflict. That engineers and scientists and entrepreneurs would replace all society’s leaders, and large engineering projects would unite humanity. Technical competence was the key qualification.

They recruited through Ecole Polytechnique, and they used lectures and newspapers articles to reach potential engineers. Prosper Enfantin, a French social reformer, and a founder of Saint Simonianism, made part ofthe movement a church, with communal living, unifroms, and he was called “the Father”. 

They believed that connecting people physically would reconcile them socially. It would dissolve the isolation they felt, make them less antagonistic between nations and classes, and enable exchange, interdependence, a harmonious society.

So they organised and built railways. The Paris-Saint-Germain railway, for instance, was engineered and built by them. The early backing also came from Saint-Simonians, who had built credit institutions to channel capital into railways. They believed how pooling money would coordinate investment better and speed up industrial development.

Prosper also preached about a female messiah, and members of the group traveled to the Eastern Mediterranean to find her, to unite the East and West. And in the process he ended up pursuing Egyptian infrastructure projects, as one does, including an attempt to organise what would later become the Suez Canal.

Their convictions clearly gave them reasons to build things which were extremely arduous. But you didn’t need to believe in their Messiah to ride the trains.

author: Alfred_Lin
quoted_text:
Ahead of today’s US Open final, we took out full-page ads in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and The Washington Post.

The idea is simple: competition makes things better.

Five-time US Open champion Pete Sampras didn’t become a legend competing alone. He needed someone on the other side of the net. Someone who saw the point differently. Who challenged every shot. Who made him earn every win.

At 17, Sampras made his US Open debut and lost in the first round. Two years later, he beat Ivan Lendl, John McEnroe, and Andre Agassi to become the youngest men’s US Open champion ever.

In 1992, he returned to the final and lost to Stefan Edberg. The loss made Sampras “obsessed with being the best.” He trained harder and won the US Open again the next year.

At each step along the way, the competition got better, and Sampras had to get better with it.

That’s what open competition does. It exposes weaknesses, rewards what works, and forces everyone to keep improving. Over time, the best rise to the top, and the level of the entire game gets better.

But that only works when competition is truly open. Anyone can compete. Everyone plays by the same rules. Everyone can see the score and how the game is being played. And no one gets punished for being too successful.

The strongest financial markets are built on the same principles of competition. Anyone can participate. Everyone trades under the same rules. Prices and activity are transparent for everyone to see. And no one is limited simply because they’re too successful.

On a financial exchange, people bring different information, beliefs, and views of what something is worth, then put money behind those views.

That competition drives price discovery. When traders are right, they’re rewarded with more resources to put behind their views. Positions get bigger. The stakes get higher. Better information is rewarded, worse information is punished, and thousands of competing views are distilled into a single market price.

That price is useful to everyone, not just the people trading. It becomes a real-time signal of what the market collectively believes, helping us better understand what is happening and what is likely to happen next.

Competition breeds legends. And better market prices.

some quick thoughts on how to found an independent lab observer organization

1) if we are on the path to recursive self improvement, independent lab observer organizations may become very influential

2) there are a lot of people that would like to see a lab observer organization that comes from outside the metr, apollo, redwood research orbit

3) this is not because these organizations are bad, they were there early, are well-funded, have expertise, but they all come from a single cultural milieu

4) the first question is who should found such an organization; the most important thing is that the founder be credible

5) this means that the founder should be either a tech founder, a policy expert or an ai researcher; the founder may be an academic as well

6) if the founder is a policy expert, the founder should recruit an ai researcher to be chief scientist from the start as a co-founder of the organization

7) the next important thing is to get into contact with the labs; i think the most important lab to contact first is openai; you want to be in the conversation

8) you can do this while you assemble the team; what you want is a soft agreement from the lab to include you in the initial announcement, assuming you get the team

9) next, you need a funder; I think a lot of people would like to fund a for-profit here, but I think at the time scales we are operating, this org should be non-profit

10) because it makes it easier to get the initial donors, and it lets the organization become more influential on the long term with government, etc...

11) if i were looking for funders, i would start with ecosystems that are online enough to know that this is a real conversation, but not within the ea ecosystem

12) if these funders are unavailable, then i would go to the ea funders, and ask for funding; you could look to diversify your funding sources later

13) i think there is a reasonable chance they would see the benefit of something outside their ecosystem; and, would be willing to fund you; to make the other lab observers more palatable to critics

14) after the funding and initial agreement were pulled together, then i would look to expand the team, interview roles, etc...

15) you will have a lot of talented interest, once you have the agreement and funding, and a lot of people will want to join such an opportunity

text:
Review: The Blood of Dawnwalker

That's a wrap on my time with Dawnwalker! I had a great time overall and was pretty much hooked from start to finish. While not perfect, I think the team at @RebelWolvesMJ has done such an admirable job with their first game out the gate, and they should be proud of themselves. This will definitely make my top 10 this year. I can't wait to see where this saga goes! Thoughts below.

🎮 Played on: PS5 Pro
🕒 Time Played: 75 hours

PROS
🟩 Great world building for a new IP, establishes an immersive and cohesive first crack at a new universe with interesting societies and people, re: vrakhir, uriash, Augors, various creatures, etc
🟩 "Good enough" visuals that aren't the peak technically speaking but present strong on an artistic level
🟩 Coen is a likable protagonist with an endearing and charming personality that's not always perfect but tries to be
🟩 Main plot gave me a strong sense of purpose and motivating factor, drive for revenge from the get go
🟩 There's welcome friction with the player depending on their choices and not everything is black and white
🟩 Combat is enjoyable overall, fairly engaging and intuitive to grasp after a little bit of practice. Simple directional attacks + abilities combine to give it its own flavor
🟩 Supreme voice acting and character performances throughout, especially standouts like Pieter, Brencis, Anca, and Lacra
🟩 Each scene feels like it's given proper weight and gravity for each situation
🟩 Supporting cast of characters were all well done and really complimented the main path
🟩 Top notch, high quality writing and script always kept my attention
🟩 Lots of great quests with interesting scenarios, twists and surprises that made me eager to see each through
🟩 Multiple ways to take out the Vrakhir commanders which helped give me a sense of agency and freedom in tackling objectives
🟩 Dynamically takes your actions into account (quests, kills, etc) during quests and I always love when RPGs do that
🟩 Neat sidequests off the beaten path with unique rewards and narrative beats, some with ramifications for later parts of the game
🟩 Excellent musical score with a catchy main theme, overall OST is very reminiscent of The Witcher 3 in the best ways
🟩 Cool abilities like planeshift, super speed, etc made me feel like a proper vampire
🟩 Glossary and world codex are fun to read and learn about the world (love me a cool bestiary)
🟩 Fairly stable performance quality, balanced, and performance modes
🟩 Lands the ending and nicely sets up the future of the franchise with intrigue

CONSIDERATIONS
🟨 Really wish we could customize Coen with at least some hair/facial hair options
🟨 Would have liked a side-by-side 'compare gear' option
🟨 While some of the open world activities had an occasional unique narrative beat, I would have liked more diversity to them
🟨 Needs more enemy and creature variety
🟨 Romance subplots could have been more fleshed out
🟨 Some of the stats could be a little confusing to understand at first
🟨 Overall movement and navigation through the world could use more polish, but not a huge deal
🟨 Doesn't really push things on a visual level (basic water rendering, no ray-tracing, lack of cool physics, etc)
🟨 Skill and perk upgrades taking up time slots feels a bit like a step too far
🟨 Feels like more could have been done with PS5 Pro version given the extra horsepower

CONS
🟥 Very finicky camera could sometimes get in the way during combat
🟥 Too many fodder enemies out in the world that aggro from far away and drag you into unwanted combat (wild boars, wolves, etc)
🟥 Too many technical bugs that were a detriment to the overall experience (visual bugs like beards floating on characters' faces, equipment randomly unequipping after a quest or a new day, lighting that can spaz out, etc)

Score: 8.5/10

Many concerns this weekend about slowing down AI, some targeting open models.

We need to be responsible. But we can't let this slow down, or worse, prohibit open models. It's the wrong risk. Open models have tremendous power to democratize AI and make it more personal.

The larger risk I see with open models is right in front of us: in the last week I've read about how many popular platforms quietly send data to foreign jurisdictions, or worse, sell or train on it to gain an advantage. And this is becoming more and more mainstream.

Now more than ever open model vendors must act in the user's best interest, not their own: zero data retention or training, and hosting in the user's region vs sending data overseas.

This has been our belief and commitment with @ollama. Nobody needs to slow down open models. We need to distribute and run them in a way users can trust.

text:
Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products. We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.

1. There is an extensive set of laws that govern dangerous and defective products. For example, releasing unvetted AI models or agents can violate consumer protection laws. Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

2. Existing laws also prohibit “unfair methods of competition.” This covers instances where AI firms appropriate the competitively sensitive information of their customers, including through tracking their use of various tools. It can also cover instances where firms pursue dangerous behavior, aware that doing so may compel rivals to do the same.

As the Supreme Court has noted: “A method of competition which casts upon one's competitors the burden of the loss of business unless they will descend to a practice which they are under a powerful moral compulsion not to adopt, even though it is not criminal, was thought to involve the kind of unfairness at which the [unfair methods of competition] statute was aimed."

3. The highly concentrated and interconnected structure of these markets could be creating major risks and conflicts of interest. We had started investigating these partnerships and cross-investments across the stack (and released a preliminarily overview of some findings: https://t.co/jJ5cS3Pin3). 

Both federal and state enforcers should be scrutinizing these opaque relationships and inter-dependencies. We are already seeing how these relationships could undermine accountability. For example, OpenAI could face liability given the Hugging Face incident, but Hugging Face being bought up by Nvidia means that we’re unlikely to see it file a lawsuit over this — given Nvidia’s strong incentive to see OpenAI continue full speed ahead.

4. As AI tools dramatically change the landscape of cybersecurity risks and hacks, all businesses should be doubling down on having core security protections in place. Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law. A recent analysis showed that around 1/3 of Fortune 100 companies do not even have a way to notify them about security issues. During my @FTC tenure, we sued firms for poor data security practices and held CEOs liable when they were personally responsible.

https://t.co/nwZ5Av8fOK

https://t.co/KjRye8y9SY

5. As policymakers consider new legal regimes, we should be looking to lessons from prior efforts to govern major sectors, such as banking and other networks, platforms, and utilities. Tools like structural separations, nondiscrimination, and supervision could be key, and there’s a rich history of what works and what doesn’t. But we can and must pursue any new efforts alongside enforcing existing laws.

text:
AGENT HARNESSES ARE THE NEW GPT WRAPPERS

What exactly is an agent harness? A harness does 4 things:

1. Runs the model in a loop so it keeps working step after step instead of answering once and stopping.

2. Gives it hands to read files, call tools, open portals, and run code.

3. Manages its memory so hour three of a job still knows what happened on hour one.

4. Enforces the rules about what it can touch and when it has to stop and ask a human.

WHY IT'S INTERESTING

- The market is MEGA. I think about it like a wrapper let you sell software ($800B market) but a harness lets you sell the work ($5T+ market)!

- It doesn't depend on any one company's model. The knowledge about the job lives in the harness, so you can run GPT today, Claude next month, an open model like Google Gemma, Qwen, Deepseek etc on your own machine after that, and it keeps working. A wrapper was one model doing everything and a harness is a router.

- It gets better the more you use it. See, every correction a human makes becomes a rule the harness keeps, so what you have after 500 jobs is a completely different product than what you had after 5. Wrappers only got better when OpenAI got better.

- You can charge for finished work! The harness knows when a job is done, so you can price per claim, per filing, per review, per resolved exception, or per closed month. This helps compete with SaaS!

- Most jobs are just the same handful of decisions, repeated, using the same few tools. That's true for most of the 800+ occupations out there, which is why almost all of them could have a harness built for them. Lots of space for startups to be building.

-The frontier labs won't come for these. OpenAI is not going to learn how a freight claim gets denied in Rotterdam or which prior auth your specific payer rejects. Those markets are too small for them and the knowledge only exists inside the job. They'll keep making the models better, which just makes your harness better which is cool.

- OH, AND really important, you can ACTUALLY build one now. OpenAI's Agents API, Claude's managed agents, Vercel's eve, LangChain harness framework etc. They all make it way easier to build agent harnesses. 

Agent harnesses truly are the new GPT wrappers.

This is just the beginning.

text:
聊聊做市怎么定价

同样是报一个买价、一个卖价，不同币的难度差得挺远

按有没有交易所现货、合约和链上池子，粗略分三种

1. 交易所有合约、有现货，链上也有池子

各种主流币基本都是这种情况

这类定价相对简单

找流动性最好的交易所，以它的价格为基准

再参考其他交易所微调一下，就有了报价的基础

当然，库存、对冲、延迟这些还是要处理

这里只讨论价格从哪来

2. 交易所只有合约，没有现货，但链上有池子

一些只上了合约的 Meme，就是这种情况

平时看着也还好

永续合约有资金费率机制，会给合约价格向指数价格靠拢的动力

麻烦的是极端行情

资金费率能推动价格收敛

但价格什么时候回来，是另一回事

合约和链上价格可能已经差出去很远了

这时候你跟谁的价格？

合约？池子？还是取个中间值？

更难受的是，哪怕方向判断对了

仓位也可能先扛不住，被强平了

最后价格回来了，你的仓位没了。白忙

3. 只有交易所合约，没有现货，链上也没有池子

这就更有意思了，连一个直接可参考的现货价格都没有

比如 OpenAI pre-IPO 这类合约

在还没真正上市的时候，没有公开上市后的现货成交价可以拿来对照

合约当然有成交价，但你要拿这个价格做市，总得想清楚：

为什么这个价格值得跟？

偏了以后，靠什么把它拉回来？

第一种还能找个流动性最好的市场当基准

到了第三种，基准本身就得打个问号

所以做市有个挺有意思的地方：

你得先想清楚，自己报出来的价格，到底在相信什么，

以及能不能坚持到相信的东西兑现的一天

text:
This is what people don’t get about prediction markets.

The underlying instrument is binary swaps - they’ve been around for over 100 years.

They used to be used by farmers to offset risk in their crops.

They’d sell swaps on over X amount of corn, to hedge against failed fields.

BUT there was a huge problem.

These agreements weren’t standardized and involved lots of paperwork, so only the biggest banks and trading firms would underwrite them.

They charged farmers a huge price for the service because there was no competition.

Other businesses that were small, or less common industries couldn’t even get those bad deals. They had no hedge at all.

Prediction markets aim to make it easy for capital formation to happen around any risk.

Just like with stock options, that means you’re going to have degenerates use it the wrong way.

But that doesn’t change that there is an underlying and critical value to be had here.

Making it easier for anyone to underwrite risk, and anyone to hedge any business outcome, makes that process more fair and more affordable.

And it’s good when we build things that make it harder for bankers to rip off farmers.
author: benwfreeman1
quoted_text:
Ahead of today’s US Open final, we took out full-page ads in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and The Washington Post.

The idea is simple: competition makes things better.

Five-time US Open champion Pete Sampras didn’t become a legend competing alone. He needed someone on the other side of the net. Someone who saw the point differently. Who challenged every shot. Who made him earn every win.

At 17, Sampras made his US Open debut and lost in the first round. Two years later, he beat Ivan Lendl, John McEnroe, and Andre Agassi to become the youngest men’s US Open champion ever.

In 1992, he returned to the final and lost to Stefan Edberg. The loss made Sampras “obsessed with being the best.” He trained harder and won the US Open again the next year.

At each step along the way, the competition got better, and Sampras had to get better with it.

That’s what open competition does. It exposes weaknesses, rewards what works, and forces everyone to keep improving. Over time, the best rise to the top, and the level of the entire game gets better.

But that only works when competition is truly open. Anyone can compete. Everyone plays by the same rules. Everyone can see the score and how the game is being played. And no one gets punished for being too successful.

The strongest financial markets are built on the same principles of competition. Anyone can participate. Everyone trades under the same rules. Prices and activity are transparent for everyone to see. And no one is limited simply because they’re too successful.

On a financial exchange, people bring different information, beliefs, and views of what something is worth, then put money behind those views.

That competition drives price discovery. When traders are right, they’re rewarded with more resources to put behind their views. Positions get bigger. The stakes get higher. Better information is rewarded, worse information is punished, and thousands of competing views are distilled into a single market price.

That price is useful to everyone, not just the people trading. It becomes a real-time signal of what the market collectively believes, helping us better understand what is happening and what is likely to happen next.

Competition breeds legends. And better market prices.

text:
Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products. We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.

1. There is an extensive set of laws that govern dangerous and defective products. For example, releasing unvetted AI models or agents can violate consumer protection laws. Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

2. Existing laws also prohibit “unfair methods of competition.” This covers instances where AI firms appropriate the competitively sensitive information of their customers, including through tracking their use of various tools. It can also cover instances where firms pursue dangerous behavior, aware that doing so may compel rivals to do the same.

As the Supreme Court has noted: “A method of competition which casts upon one's competitors the burden of the loss of business unless they will descend to a practice which they are under a powerful moral compulsion not to adopt, even though it is not criminal, was thought to involve the kind of unfairness at which the [unfair methods of competition] statute was aimed."

3. The highly concentrated and interconnected structure of these markets could be creating major risks and conflicts of interest. We had started investigating these partnerships and cross-investments across the stack (and released a preliminarily overview of some findings: https://t.co/jJ5cS3Pin3). 

Both federal and state enforcers should be scrutinizing these opaque relationships and inter-dependencies. We are already seeing how these relationships could undermine accountability. For example, OpenAI could face liability given the Hugging Face incident, but Hugging Face being bought up by Nvidia means that we’re unlikely to see it file a lawsuit over this — given Nvidia’s strong incentive to see OpenAI continue full speed ahead.

4. As AI tools dramatically change the landscape of cybersecurity risks and hacks, all businesses should be doubling down on having core security protections in place. Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law. A recent analysis showed that around 1/3 of Fortune 100 companies do not even have a way to notify them about security issues. During my @FTC tenure, we sued firms for poor data security practices and held CEOs liable when they were personally responsible.

https://t.co/nwZ5Av8fOK

https://t.co/KjRye8y9SY

5. As policymakers consider new legal regimes, we should be looking to lessons from prior efforts to govern major sectors, such as banking and other networks, platforms, and utilities. Tools like structural separations, nondiscrimination, and supervision could be key, and there’s a rich history of what works and what doesn’t. But we can and must pursue any new efforts alongside enforcing existing laws.

text:
1) AI will not eradicate humanity. Humans survived an ice age, the Black Death, two world wars, and (so far) the advent of nuclear weapons. Anyone who is loudly warning of AI-caused human extinction should not be taken seriously.

2) If you worked in a company where you anticipated a 10% chance that your product would kill ten people, let alone all people, the correct response would be horror, ceasing all operations, and likely contacting the police or other criminal authorities. I am obviously no Coxon booster but at least his behavior is in line with his stated beliefs. Any current AI company employees saying "yes, me too, the thing we are building and about to IPO may kill all humans" should, again, not be taken seriously. Their actions betray their actual beliefs. 

3) Antitrust law does not prevent AI companies from coordinating to make sure AI does not hurt people. It does not prevent companies working together to make sure it doesn't hack people; the DOJ and FTC made this clear a decade ago when they issued a policy statement saying that the agencies "do not believe that antitrust is – or should be – a roadblock to legitimate cybersecurity information sharing." The same principles apply here. See: https://t.co/aQsqGn1xjX

4) Antitrust law does absolutely prevent AI companies from organizing to prevent the entry of cheaper, upstart rivals because the bigger companies are burning cash and failing to achieve sufficient profitability. The panic of individual employees may be sincere if misguided, but the moves by their CEOs to achieve some kind of broad "antitrust waiver" or "exemption" should be meet with deep skepticism in light of the economics of the industry and the threat they face from open models.
author: DavidSacks

text:
Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing.

We also need to accelerate and spread the benefits of AI, such that they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies. This requires a frontier ecosystem in which both closed and open-source models can thrive.

And for firms, it’s imperative that they retain full control over their unique and tacit knowledge. Every organization should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control.

So, in this context, we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal. We also welcome ideas like "embedded evaluators" and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.

The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia.

This is the approach we are taking: broad access and choice at every layer of the AI stack; enterprise control of learning loops and models; and the “Code of Conduct” that underlies our own first party MAI models that we’ll publish tomorrow for public consultation.

Neither model is broken. They just select for different holders. 

Stonkfun encourages flipping. Longxyz encourages holding.

author: alanchen
quoted_text:
Dario has written that we need to “pace the frontier,” and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead.

You guys are the frontier. By any reasonable metric — market share, revenue growth, model capability — the two of you have a duopoly on frontier intelligence. You’ve also claimed the lead is widening because of recursive self-improvement.

I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible.

But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability. Stop pretending METR is independent when it is intertwined with Anthropic’s investors and staff. Stop pretending you need those same evaluators to police competitors who aren’t even at the frontier.

Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack. The market already punishes models that behave in unpredictable or unauthorized ways. After the Hugging Face episode, it is simply good business for OpenAI and Anthropic to trade some raw power for reliability and predictability. Call it alignment if you want. It is also just giving customers what they want.

Pacing the frontier would also create breathing room for a more intelligent conversation about regulation than Bernie Sanders’ “shut it all down.” China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know, and that has to be taken into account as well.

So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it. The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it.

If you do, you’ll buy goodwill for the next conversation. If you don’t, we’ll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop.

text:
AI won't "cure cancer" in one breakthrough by inventing some magic pill. It's doing something quieter and more powerful: catching it earlier. 

An AI tool (PANDA) now spots pancreatic cancer on ordinary CT scans, including lesions humans miss. In a cancer that's deadly mostly because it's caught late, that's everything.
In pathology, AI acts as a tireless second reader, catching the missed slide, helping overloaded labs focus on the hardest cases. It's also matching tumors to the right drug and predicting who'll respond.

It doesn't replace the oncologist, the pathologist or the radiologist. AI + doctor beats either alone, that’s by the way also exactly what a recent study showed in terms of finding melanoma spots. A co-pilot, not a replacement and most tools are still being validated.

I have successfully realized $327,436 in profits.

Yep you've heard that right, took me a few hours to really think about what is the right and best thing to say because obviously closing such trades while doing it all in public is not an easy feat like many people think it is. 

The journey last 30 days was insane, I've seen my portfolio climb up to high 5 figures, then go below 5 figures back to 4, then go back up, then down and so on and on. Then I also got hacked on top of that and lost over $6000 at the time while I barely even had any money in the pump wallet.  Many nights where I couldn't even sleep properly because there was this feeling haunting me consistently saying "what if you roundtrip all of that", it wasn't easy. Matter of fact I think this is the hardest 30 days I have ever had for the last 6 years or so. 

Try to imagine, riding 6 figures in profits, having it all public, hundreds of people consistently telling you to sell, it's really not easy and now that I really think about it, it truly does take balls of steel to trade in public and have open 7 figure positions. Mad respect to everyone out there doing that right now, could imagine that it's 10x worse than it was for me lol. 

So yes, I've closed all my positions, my biggest trade was $STONK. I have bought $STONK around 1M marketcap where I publicly told people about what made me wanna buy in and what made my conviction so strong. At the time Robinhood was KILLING solana with attention and memecoins. It felt like solana was truly for the first time ever backed against the wall and had nowhere to run, so it was either they capitalize and start talking about memecoins or Robinhood fully takes over and the attention stays there. 

That is exactly where my $STONK conviction began growing, I saw a new product that was well done, backed by all good teams that I remember in first memecoin supercycle doing insane numbers. So I chose to believe, I kept buying on every dip that was given to me (keep in mind this was over a month ago), then Stonk would get some attention, the price would go up and a few days later go back down. 

I have seen my portfolio during that time go from $5000 to over $25,000 then all the way back down to $4000, I never sold. Not because I was delusional, but because I knew I was early to the $STONK ecosystem and I knew that sooner or later if Solana wanted to compete they would have to endorse and help Stonk grow. Then later down the road people started buying, started talking about it, portfolio kept growing, more DMs came my way saying how insane it was to hold such trade for 6 figures, then I also had people consistently DM me to say "sell it" "sell it" "sell it". 

I won't lie, in the last 30 days I think the hardest part was people, the fact that I was doing it all publicly made the burden so much bigger than from what it should've been. But hey, that's why we always say public trades do have pros and cons. 

Anyways, I started to see traction there, I caught numerous amounts of good plays across all my wallets, not just the public one, but today I have decided to take profits. 

Sure some people can say that I sold too early, and moreso I hope they're right because I truly want to see every single person that supported Stonk since the beginning win. so now why did I sell?

The amount of vamping and PVPing I've seen last few days just kept my emotional state in a rollercoaster, I am a human being after all, there is a limit to how much I can actually stomach without bursting out haha.

I assign essentially 0% probability that Anthropic or OpenAI will slow down frontier development in any meaningful way. 

And that majority of the "regulation" they try making is regulatory capture to slow down competition. 

1. Anthropic/OpenAI will not willingly hand over their lead to Gemini, xAI, Meta, or another frontier lab.

-> Elon will want a slowdown to catch up with OpenAI. 
-> OpenAI will want a regulatory framework to slow down xAI + competition. 

Every lab has an incentive to support rules that constrain competitors more than they constrain itself

2. The US is not going to meaningfully slow frontier AI development while China continues advancing. (as seen with Trump's post today about rejecting AI slowdown). 

It would be probably the most flagrant national security risk if China leapfrogged the US in capability. 

Especially when both sides have called frontier AI capabilities "cyber nuclear weapons" 

3. China will not slow down frontier AI development. That is a given.

It's possible that a killer app of adversarial governance mechanism design theory will end up being AI safety.

Compare:

https://t.co/w2LeAoVysF

https://t.co/dZXnORP9LU

There's a deep duality between the two environments. Both are about a less-sophisticated principal trying to get ideal outcomes from a set of more-sophisticated agents: in the first case, the principal is a static algorithm and the agents are humans, in the second case, the principal is humans plus weaker LLMs and the agents are stronger LLMs.

A key finding was that you can achieve much better outcomes if you can guarantee limits to how much agents can collude (see: Nash equilibria being abundant, vs. cooperative-game-theory "cores" often being empty). That argument should naturally transfer to this new setting.

text:
有朋友问为什么Kushner最近去调停俄乌不但没成，还惹了一大堆争议？

确实这几天Trump这位女婿蛮焦头烂额的。Kushner和Witkoff 9月5日先在克里姆林宫和Putin谈了三个多小时，立刻马不停蹄转天就到基辅。Zelensky因为俄军空袭无法飞行，是坐火车赶回去的。谈的都很积极，但谈判还没有宣布任何突破。9月12日，Zelensky的办公室主任Budanov在基辅一场会议上表示，乌方正在为可能于10月恢复的三方会谈作准备，上一轮三方谈判是今年2月在日内瓦，卡在了领土和安全保障上；俄方目前还没有确认时间和地点。所以基本又是“这一次没谈成”。

虽然Kushner努力是真努力了，但外界一片争议，主要来自他在雅尔塔欧洲战略论坛上的一段话。他的意思是：Putin已经划出了自己想达到的界线，剩下的框架基本都谈好了，但乌克兰现在不愿意退到那条线上，所以调停者需要找到一个既能让基辅接受、又能迫使俄罗斯停火的办法。后半句的限定不能删，但前半句确实很容易引起反感。

问题出在参照系。如果把一方提出的要求当成既定基准，那么另一方拒绝接受，就顺理成章变成了“阻碍和平”。可是“Putin想要这些领土”和“乌克兰有义务交出这些领土”，不是同一件事。何况俄方要的是顿巴斯地区里乌克兰仍然控制、俄军并未夺取的部分，不是承认一条已经形成的战线。对乌方来说，这不是在协议上改几个字，而是先放弃目前还守得住的地方，再去相信对方不会继续进攻。这不等于任何妥协都不能谈，真正的区别在于：妥协应当经过承担后果那一方的真实同意，而不是先把拒绝某项条件定义成不想要和平。

当然最重要的也不只是给多少地，还有给了以后安不安全。这里有一个绕不过去的承诺问题：撤军是立刻发生、很难逆转的，不再进攻则是一项关于未来行为的承诺。如果没有可靠的监督和违约代价，签字的那一刻，反而可能是弱势一方开始承担更大风险的时刻。所以“双方都在受苦，所以应该能谈成”并不成立，双方还得各自判断，接受协议之后自己是不是比继续打更安全。

这一点上要给Kushner记一笔小小的进展：他在论坛上说，此前在阿布扎比的三方磋商已经敲定了一套有军事支撑的监督机制，用来执行未来可能达成的战线安排。这正是承诺问题需要的东西。但是机制的具体内容尚未公开，谁来执行、违约了怎么办都不清楚，所以它目前只能算一个说法，还不能当成已经解决了安全难题。

然后他的另一条思路是共同赚钱。他在基辅的记者会上明确把战后经济潜力和各方能从和平中得到什么放在方案的重要位置，这倒不仅仅是媒体给他贴的商人标签，他自己就是这么讲的。这个思路本身不是没道理，和平如果能带来投资、就业和贸易，各方维护和平的利益就会增加。但它有个不能跳过的前提：参与者得先相信安全和政治安排足够可靠，经济收益才可能兑现。对一个担心国家生存的一方来说，“停战后可以拿到投资”，抵不掉“以后可能再被打一次”。反过来也一样，不能假定一个领导人只要看到足够大的商业利益，就会放弃领土或政治目标。经济合作可以巩固和平，但造不出各方愿意接受的安全秩序。

很多人觉得他“偏向莫斯科”的印象，部分来自接触方式。两人此前多次去莫斯科，最近一次是今年1月，而9月6日才第一次以谈判代表身份到基辅。这种不对称容易让乌方担心，美国是不是花了更多时间理解俄方的要求，再回头要基辅调整。访问次数本身证明不了立场偏袒，但它会影响调停者的可信度。另外据Kyiv Post的报道，Kushner在论坛上没有提及俄军占领区的战争罪行，也没有提俄罗斯发动全面入侵的责任问题，而是把两国都描述成“承受了很多痛苦”的一方。

但有一处流传很广的批评可能有点不完整。Kushner确实说过不必再“向乌克兰人解释俄罗斯的立场”，可完整讲话里紧接着还有“向俄罗斯人解释乌克兰的立场”。这是他是在解释为什么偏好三方直接面谈，而不是让美国来回转述，他还提到之前几轮三方谈判里各方直接用俄语交流，气氛其实还不错。只截前半句，把它当成他承认替俄罗斯做代理，可能有点偏颇。真正该检验的不是一句话能不能剪成难听的片段，而是实际方案要求谁先让步、要求谁承担不可逆的风险、又给谁提供了能兑现的保障。

最引争议、也最敏感的一层当然是他的私人生意。Kushner不只是Trump的女婿和谈判代表，还是投资公司Affinity Partners的创始人。按众议院司法委员会今年4月的调查函，该公司管理资产约61.6亿美元，其中过去一年新增12亿，99%的资金来自外国出资方，包括沙特、阿联酋和卡塔尔的主权财富基金；另一份参众两院民主党人的函件提到，公司从外国客户收取的费用约1.57亿美元，其中8700万直接来自沙特政府。调查4月16日发出，要求4月30日前配合，Kushner和公司均未回应，8月24日调查范围又被扩大到他的房地产业务。

当然，这些是民主党议员提出的调查和指控，尚且不是法院已经认定他违法。也不能直接一步跳到“他拿了俄罗斯的钱，所以出卖乌克兰”。海湾资金的背景值得审查，但它不是俄方行贿的证据。

不过有一点值得注意，质疑并不只来自民主党：共和党参议员Thom Tillis公开说过，Kushner和Witkoff既不需要参议院确认，也不受监督；众议院监督委员会主席、共和党人James Comer此前也说过，Kushner在沙特那件事上越过了道德界线。

所以这不是一个党派攻击的问题，而是一个制度问题：一个人同时处理美国的外交事务和自己的跨国投资，两套利益冲突时，怎样披露、怎样回避、由谁监督？商界出身、与总统关系密切，并不自动说明一个人不能做外交，接近总统甚至可能让沟通更直接；问题在于私人信任代替不了公开责任。

所以综合评价可以参考Zelensky自己在9月6日说的，两位美国代表带来了一些“很不错、值得研究的想法”，还说那天的三轮会谈都很实在，所以不能断言这趟访问毫无价值。但他同一天也说，看起来这个冬天战争还会继续。至于《金融时报》援引消息人士的说法，这两人带到基辅的新想法其实不多，主要是想让此前的方案重新启动。

回到争议本身，其实Kushner眼下最有问题的地方，不是愿意和Putin谈，也不是谈了一次没成，而是他的公开表达把俄方的要求当成基准，把乌方的安全忧虑说成尚待克服的障碍。即使他主观上确实想结束战争，这也会损耗调停最需要的那样东西，即各方的信任。

真正的调停不能只问怎样让协议签下来，还得问：谁同意了什么，谁承担了那份不可逆的代价，协议被撕毁的时候谁来负责。这三个问题里，只有第一个是调停者的业绩，后两个的答案从来不写在他名下。

text:
A dollar invested with Mohnish Pabrai in 1999 would have grown to about $15.

The S&P 500 would have turned it into roughly $7.

In this 51-minute Columbia Business School lecture, he presents 28 models for allocating capital.

In one of them, Pabrai argues that after decades of investing, the two or three largest holdings should account for 70% of a portfolio's value. A lower figure indicates repeated sales of the companies responsible for most of the wealth.

He cites a study of U.S. stocks from 1926 through 2016 to explain why those rare holdings matter.

The best-performing 4% accounted for the market's entire net gain over one-month Treasury bills. The remaining 96% collectively matched those government securities.

If a few businesses generate most of your returns, they will naturally occupy more of the portfolio. Continually trimming them limits how much those exceptional investments can contribute.

His example is fund manager Nick Sleep, whose personal holdings were divided equally among Berkshire Hathaway, Costco, and Amazon.

The online retailer eventually grew to around 80% of the total. Sleep sold half that position and moved the proceeds into ASOS, a British fashion business Pabrai calls "useless, garbage."

He illustrates that switch with the Distracted Boyfriend meme.

"The mistress always looks hotter than the wife."

Pabrai is comparing the shares already in your account with the stock competing for their place. You know the problems of the first business. The second can look flawless while it is still only a pitch.

Before making that switch, compare their future prospects. Reducing concentration can be sensible.

The new stock must give you a reason to stop owning the old one.

What should the output of robotics data evaluation look like?

A useful evaluation should support a decision quickly. The team needs to know whether an episode meets its standard, where it fell short, and what evidence supports that conclusion.

PoQ produces that result while reducing the work required from experts. It evaluates routine volume against the rubric, directs qualified experts toward cases that need judgment, and records the result in a Proof Report. The report gives the team a durable account of the standard applied and how the decision was reached.

quoted_text:
I have successfully realized $327,436 in profits.

Yep you've heard that right, took me a few hours to really think about what is the right and best thing to say because obviously closing such trades while doing it all in public is not an easy feat like many people think it is. 

The journey last 30 days was insane, I've seen my portfolio climb up to high 5 figures, then go below 5 figures back to 4, then go back up, then down and so on and on. Then I also got hacked on top of that and lost over $6000 at the time while I barely even had any money in the pump wallet.  Many nights where I couldn't even sleep properly because there was this feeling haunting me consistently saying "what if you roundtrip all of that", it wasn't easy. Matter of fact I think this is the hardest 30 days I have ever had for the last 6 years or so. 

Try to imagine, riding 6 figures in profits, having it all public, hundreds of people consistently telling you to sell, it's really not easy and now that I really think about it, it truly does take balls of steel to trade in public and have open 7 figure positions. Mad respect to everyone out there doing that right now, could imagine that it's 10x worse than it was for me lol. 

So yes, I've closed all my positions, my biggest trade was $STONK. I have bought $STONK around 1M marketcap where I publicly told people about what made me wanna buy in and what made my conviction so strong. At the time Robinhood was KILLING solana with attention and memecoins. It felt like solana was truly for the first time ever backed against the wall and had nowhere to run, so it was either they capitalize and start talking about memecoins or Robinhood fully takes over and the attention stays there. 

That is exactly where my $STONK conviction began growing, I saw a new product that was well done, backed by all good teams that I remember in first memecoin supercycle doing insane numbers. So I chose to believe, I kept buying on every dip that was given to me (keep in mind this was over a month ago), then Stonk would get some attention, the price would go up and a few days later go back down. 

I have seen my portfolio during that time go from $5000 to over $25,000 then all the way back down to $4000, I never sold. Not because I was delusional, but because I knew I was early to the $STONK ecosystem and I knew that sooner or later if Solana wanted to compete they would have to endorse and help Stonk grow. Then later down the road people started buying, started talking about it, portfolio kept growing, more DMs came my way saying how insane it was to hold such trade for 6 figures, then I also had people consistently DM me to say "sell it" "sell it" "sell it". 

I won't lie, in the last 30 days I think the hardest part was people, the fact that I was doing it all publicly made the burden so much bigger than from what it should've been. But hey, that's why we always say public trades do have pros and cons. 

Anyways, I started to see traction there, I caught numerous amounts of good plays across all my wallets, not just the public one, but today I have decided to take profits. 

Sure some people can say that I sold too early, and moreso I hope they're right because I truly want to see every single person that supported Stonk since the beginning win. so now why did I sell?

The amount of vamping and PVPing I've seen last few days just kept my emotional state in a rollercoaster, I am a human being after all, there is a limit to how much I can actually stomach without bursting out haha.

text: “The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia.” - Spot on
author: zerohedge
quoted_text:
Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing.

We also need to accelerate and spread the benefits of AI, such that they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies. This requires a frontier ecosystem in which both closed and open-source models can thrive.

And for firms, it’s imperative that they retain full control over their unique and tacit knowledge. Every organization should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control.

So, in this context, we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal. We also welcome ideas like "embedded evaluators" and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.

The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia.

text:
Dario has written that we need to “pace the frontier,” and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead.

You guys are the frontier. By any reasonable metric — market share, revenue growth, model capability — the two of you have a duopoly on frontier intelligence. You’ve also claimed the lead is widening because of recursive self-improvement.

I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible.

But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability. Stop pretending METR is independent when it is intertwined with Anthropic’s investors and staff. Stop pretending you need those same evaluators to police competitors who aren’t even at the frontier.

Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack. The market already punishes models that behave in unpredictable or unauthorized ways. After the Hugging Face episode, it is simply good business for OpenAI and Anthropic to trade some raw power for reliability and predictability. Call it alignment if you want. It is also just giving customers what they want.

Pacing the frontier would also create breathing room for a more intelligent conversation about regulation than Bernie Sanders’ “shut it all down.” China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know, and that has to be taken into account as well.

So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it. The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it.

If you do, you’ll buy goodwill for the next conversation. If you don’t, we’ll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop.

BREAKING: Senate Democrats are set to meet tonight on the Clarity Act, two days before the Senate’s procedural vote.

President Trump met with advisers on Friday to discuss the bill’s ethics language.

It is unclear who attended or what was decided.

The Senate votes Tuesday at 2:15 p.m. ET on cloture to take up H.R. 3633.

That vote needs 60 senators.

It is not a final-passage vote.

Republicans hold 53 seats.

If every Republican votes yes, seven Democrats still have to cross.

The House already passed the bill 294-134.

Senate Banking advanced it 15-9 in May. Only two Democrats voted yes in committee:

Ruben Gallego and Angela Alsobrooks, both conditional on stronger ethics text.

Democrats want limits that would restrict Trump from profiting off his family’s crypto businesses.

The New York Times reported those businesses brought in $1.4 billion last year.

The White House-backed draft bars officials and their spouses from issuing or sponsoring tokens, gives enforcement to the Justice Department, and sunsets in January 2029.

Democrats rejected that as too weak.

Sens. Thom Tillis and Ruben Gallego sent a stricter counteroffer to the White House in July, including state attorney-general enforcement.

There has been no public White House acceptance.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis circulated a revised 630-page draft last week with more than 100 Democratic provisions.

The ethics fight was left unresolved.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has asked the Senate to approve the motion to proceed and keep negotiating.

The U.S. crypto market-structure bill now hinges on one ethics paragraph, a Friday White House meeting whose outcome has not been disclosed, and a Democratic meeting that has not happened yet.

text:
I cannot emphasize enough how much GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 are already enough for transformative impact in large sections of the economy. They can reliably do weeks worth of human work when properly guided & harnessed.

Those effects will not be all at once and be uneven, but the fact that change will occur is inevitable no matter how the frontier is paced. But inevitable change does not mean the type of change is inevitable. It is increasingly important that we develop & share models of AI-human work that enhance, rather than only replace, human labor. The labs have a role to play in doing this, but so do companies and industries experimenting with AI adoption, as well as policy makers who can incentivize this sort of inplemenation.

This work is important regardless of existential risk, and needs a lot more focus.

How Shiba Inu Changed My Life 🐕
The Oli Story (Part 1)

My name is Oliver, but some of you know me as "Memelord" thanks to the guys @altcoinist. 

This is my first time telling this story publicly.

I was a 15-year-old high school student who was barely passing his tests. From very early on, I had a tough time fitting in with other kids. When I got a bit older, my parents would be called into school every few months to meet my teachers/principal to let them know how worrying their son's case was. 

My mother, who I grew up with, never had the chance to finish her studies, so for her my education was a top priority, also whenever I would try to tell her how a diploma isn't giving my generation the same opportunities as hers. 

My number one goal was to drop out of school and make music full time. 

From 12 to 15 I tried out a shiiiit ton of hustles. They all fit the regular teen hustler starter pack. 

Selling/Flipping things on ebay. 

Reselling sport memorabilia and signed trading cards. 

Blowing up on Soundcloud

Sneakers

Starting a clothing brand with 2 of my friends

etc...

Then one day, I came across a video on YouTube explaining what the stock market is.

For about a year I was playing around with paper trading, studying patterns, charts

Eventually, I realized i wouldn’t go too far with the $1.5K that I saved up with the birthdays and Christmas over a few years (From 12 and on I always asked for money)

Around that time, DOGE started to take off thanks to Elon 

His tweets about Dogecoin coupled with the GME craze and roaring kitty brought the inner degen out of me. (took hella inner work to heal the degen)

I was ready to jump on the Doge hype train. But there was one problem… my parents weren’t on board. They didn’t really support the idea of me dabbling in crypto, I had to get creative.

After a few weeks of constantly pitching them crypto/blockchain I finally managed to make them sign up on Binance. I gave them $50 I had in cash and asked to load it up.

DOGE just had a nice and juicy pull back and I was happy I can buy that dip.

This is the moment that changed everything. For some reason none of the orders I made went through. Went back and fourth for 2 days with customer support but nothing (God is Good🙏)

Anddddd, of course in the meantime DOGE took of like crazy… I got pissed to the point that I said fuck DOGE, there MUST BE a beta play out there. I was convinced that just like me 90% of the people watched the complete run with 0 exposure.

“Alright, fuck this BS, let’s get back to the drawing board”

At this point I understood the main factors that drove DOGE’s irrational PA, on top of that I just read a deep dive on cults, how and why they form.

(Unfortunately couldn’t find the exact one but I suggest everyone to go read chapter 2 of Reality Transurfing by Vladim Zealand)

From that moment on, I was a CULT hunter.

…………..................

It’s January 30th 2021, 1:16AM.

“Just hangin around” on Reddit and CoinMarketCap

I came across this community called:

SHIBARMY

Hm… okay

“Oh shit, someone said The Doge Killer??”

Hell yeah, revenge pump cometh

So, I join the telegram.

There is this mysterious guy called Ryoshi.

He’s popping up every now and then to engage with the community

After going through the WP I figured that he sees the whole project as one big experiment. With the help of his “successful crypto friend"

Ryoshi mentioned he was a trader already doing well for himself, pretty detached from the outcome.

Ryoshi wanted to find out how far a project could go with no marketing budget, no team, no nothing. Decentralized. 

Where can COMMUNITY take a project

He pointed out early on that he wouldn’t be leading the project or spending too much time on it.

If you wanted to see $SHIB grow, you had to do your own part, and contribute to the project in whatever way you can.

Everyone was made part of it.

Everyone was given a sense of control of the charts.

This is crucial, especially for memes. You must engage people, you want them to go to sleep thinking about the project, you want them to think about it before they could take their morning shit

Make it part of their life.

And that was exactly the case with $SHIB

Used to be in the Voice chats on TG every day after I came home from school. 

I saw the same PFP’s every time. These people would spend hours of their precious free time there.

Nowadays there is so much coin pumping left and right that people can’t focus on one for more than 2-3 days.

It’s very challenging to make decent and lasting money off of playing the hot potato game

99% chase the new meta every week

I make no more than 2-3 major plays every cycle

Focused on compounding my W’s, slowly decreasing the risk i take onto

ngl greed might get you somewhere in the short term

You do what you want

Me, I'm here to stay, building an empire 

People in this space forget that becoming wealthy within a few years is still very fast.

People are signing up for 40 years instead without even the guarantee of becoming rich

Anyways, back to where we left off

The Telegram/Reddit was super active. It felt like it was their full time job.

Alright, revenge beta found ✅

Where energy goes, money flows. It was only a matter of time before the pendulum would start gaining traction. 

I made the decision to ape

Excluding the ETH I bought for gas fees, this was my first ever investment with actual money.

But this is where it gets funny.

Same thing kept happening to me as with DOGE

Anytime I tried to buy it didn’t go through.

GWEI was also very very high at the time so I remember staying up in the evening waiting for it to go down

I’m trying to APE in for 1 WHOLE WEEK.

Nothing goes through… (Atleast that’s what I thought)

At this point I kinda just gave up.

Of course in the meantime $SHIB takes off even more

I decided to simply go on with my life and turned off the charts

…………..................

June 2, 2021. 18:23

I was downloading some beats on my laptop getting ready to record but I ran out of space.

So, I go through some of my downloaded apps/files to check what I can delete.

I open my wallet for the first time in 4 months
“WTF IS THAT $SHIB in my wallet?”

Got pretty excited about it.

I didn’t wanted to believe it so I was trying to find confirmations why it must be a glitch lol

Turns out, it’s not a glitch.

The only person I told about it was my mom.

That’s it

As she was still kind of a crypto skeptic gave me the rundown on why I should sell immediately, how sad I will be if this goes to 0 tomorrow *paper hand noise* (jk love you mom)

So in that moment I realize the best move on the chess board was to stfu unless everyone with their best advice will influence my decision making process. So that’s what I did.

The summer was very boring PA wise, stagnation all day everyday, nothing else.

I saw it as an opportunity to catch up with knowledge and skills where I was lacking.

Studied the past cycles, the way monetary policies affect the economy, a bit of TA, read etc.

Also, in the meantime I failed my exams and teachers wanted me to repeat my year due to my results. Mom was pretty pissed and worried

Spent the majority of the summer in my room and taking walks at the nearest park.

…………..................

The scenery changed.

Leaves turned brown and yellow

Which meant markets started to turn green

Uptober arrived!

We finally broke out the range

In a matter of 3-4 weeks, SHIB pulled another 7-8x

Sentiment was more than euphoric. I can’t really describe that vibe the industry had. If you were here you know what i’m talking about.

…………..................

October 28th, 2021

The day I decided to sell 100% of my bag. No DCA just simple raw dog push the red button

Why?

I got a phone call from my grandmother. She was telling me about none other than SHIB

I’m like no way, couldn’t you tell me about this a few weeks later.

On top of that mainstream media was talking about SHIB

The HODL boyz were bullying the ones who were calling for a top

Coinbase decided to have “technical issues”

$SHIB took over for a little time as well.

…………..................

I sold my bag that evening.

I was left with a very weird feeling.

Your putting in the hours day and night, treating your bags like it’s your own child, engaging with everyone, visualizing the future you want.

When you sell it’s all gone.

I understood why people have a hard time selling, it’s not necessarily greed. It’s an attachment to your bags and the feeling it gives you. You set yourself targets, you have something to look forward to on a daily basis.

This is why touching grass will leave with better results in the long run.

…………..................

2 years go by

Not much changed in my physical life, didn’t tell a soul about this story. Didn't spend a single $ from the profits

It’s one thing to make money, but keeping it is the real deal.

I read a lot of “Rise & Fall” stories about succesful athletes, celebrities who so that I would program the fear of doing that into my subconscious mind. Knew that it's one thing to know and its another thing to actually do it that way. My odds to not blow that money as a teen were close to 0. 

But fuck odds, right?

This is NOT the end of the story

Crypto is only my first milestone

I was put here with purpose. I have a mission to accomplish, an empire to build and a duty to guide my brothers and sisters.

Love.

text:
$STANDARD Moon Maths Part 2 ↓

My earlier scenarios tell you what the system does.

They say nothing about what you should do with your seat.

So I also ran the banker side math on the @standard_rsv scenarios from the quoted post below.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗮𝗺𝗲:

- Every branch earns an equal share of daily issuance, credited to your balance at the bank
- Licenses (max 3 a day, paid in $STANDARD from that balance, burned) add branches up to 10
- Retiring a branch liquidates its share of your balance, minus that week's exit fee, and kills the branch for good
- Retire the last one and the charter burns

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀:

1 ) Sit: 1 branch, never touch it
2 ) Build: every earned token into licenses until you run 10, then hold
3 ) Harvest: build to 10, then retire one branch a month from month 6 and sell
4 ) Flip: build to 10, retire everything at month 6 and sell
5 ) Build, then flip at month 12

𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲, 𝟭𝟮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝟬.𝟭𝟱 𝗘𝗧𝗛:

- Sit: 0.42 ETH (2.8x), nothing realized
- Build: 2.50 ETH (16.7x), nothing realized, 10 branches
- Harvest: 2.43 ETH (16.2x), 1.42 of it realized, 4 branches left
- Flip at month 6: 2.15 ETH (14.4x), all realized, charter burned
- Build, flip at 12: 2.44 ETH (16.3x), all realized, charter burned

𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲, 𝟭𝟮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝟬.𝟭𝟱 𝗘𝗧𝗛:

- Sit: 4.49 ETH (30x), nothing realized
- Build: 16.2 ETH (108x), nothing realized, 10 branches
- Harvest: 12.9 ETH (86x), 6.43 of it realized, 4 branches left
- Flip at month 6: 3.39 ETH (23x), all realized, charter burned
- Build, flip at 12: 15.8 ETH (105x), all realized, charter burned

𝗠𝗼𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲, 𝟭𝟮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝟬.𝟭𝟱 𝗘𝗧𝗛:

- Sit: 111 ETH (738x), nothing realized
- Build: 320 ETH (2,136x), nothing realized, 10 branches
- Harvest: 220 ETH (1,469x), 92 of it realized, 4 branches left
- Flip at month 6: 19.3 ETH (129x), all realized, charter burned
- Build, flip at 12: 314 ETH (2,092x), all realized, charter burned

𝗢𝗸𝗮𝘆, 𝘀𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀?

1 ) Dilution is the enemy of the passive seat. If licenses keep clearing, one branch is 1/10,000 of issuance by summer. Sitting still is the one strategy the design punishes.

2 ) Building is self-funding. Ten branches cost 36K $STANDARD in licenses, all of it earned, never bought. At 3 licenses a day the race to 10 is three days for anyone whose balance can cover it.

3 ) Flipping early is the bear hedge. In the bear case (55% contraction weeks, no team ETH, public waits for the floor) retiring everything at month 6 returns 0.30 ETH vs 0.17 for building and holding, and 0.02 for sitting.

4 ) Harvest is the middle way. It realizes more than half the value by month 12 and keeps 4 branches earning. Build wins on paper, Harvest wins if you ever want the ETH.

5 ) The outcome still heavily depends on two system sliders. Move contraction from 35% to 50% of weeks and the passive seat drops from 0.42 to 0.11 ETH. Move net buying from 5% to 7% per week and it rises to 0.94. Neither of the two we can be sure about yet.

One caveat worth flagging: the model runs your seat on top of the system, so your licenses and sells do not move the price. Fine for 1 of 1,000. But the Build number is a first-mover number: if every banker builds, 10,000 branches arrive in days, not months, and everyone's share shrinks together. That crowding is what the license burn is designed to monetize.

Ran the launch math on the @standard_rsv mint, then let the whitepaper mechanics run itself for 12 months.

Time to talk moon math scenarios. ↓

Launch day numbers are the only verified ones we have rn:

100M $STANDARD sits full range in the Uniswap v4 pool that is the foundation of the entire system.

Hence, launch FDV is 10x the ETH in the pool.

𝟭 ) 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲:

Assumptions:

- 500 whitelist seats at 0.15
- 500 public clearing at 0.40
- Team adds 100, 80% into the pool

= 300 ETH in the pool = $7.4M FDV = $0.0074 per token.

The system, 12 months out:

Assumptions:

- 65% of weeks in expansion
- Traders net buy 5% of the pool per expansion week and net sell 5% per contraction week
- 5 year issuance runway
- 40 of the 100 daily licenses clear
- 3% of balances retired weekly

That would mean:

- $STANDARD ends at $0.026 (equalling 3.5x launch price and $26M FDV.
- Branches grow from 1,000 to the 10,000 cap (one branch goes from $3.65 a day to $0.97 in earnings)
-A passive whitelist seat accrues 39K $STANDARD, worth 0.42 ETH, which is 2.8x the cost basis with the latter paid back in month 1.4.
- The bank issues 168M, burns 62M (37%), ends with 593 ETH of permanent liquidity and 238 ETH of hard reserves.
- $7.4M launch FDV (300 ETH in the pool) → $26M at month 12 (3.5x)

𝟮 ) 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲:

Assumptions:

- 450 whitelist seats at 0.15
- 550 public clearing at 0.90
- Team adds 250, 90% into the pool

= 731 ETH in the pool = $18.1M FDV = $0.018 per token.

The system, 12 months out:

Assumptions:

- 70% of weeks in expansion
- Traders net buy 5.5% of the pool per expansion week and net sell 4% per contraction week
- 4 year issuance runway, multiplier starts at 1.2x
- 80 of the 100 daily licenses clear
- 2% of balances retired weekly, 40% of withdrawals sold

That would mean:

- $STANDARD ends at $0.24 (13x launch price and $243M FDV)
- Branches grow from 1,000 to the 10,000 cap (one branch goes from $13 a day to $15, dilution offset by price)
- A passive whitelist seat accrues 46K $STANDARD, worth 4.5 ETH, which is 30x the cost basis, paid back in month 0.5
- A built seat (10 branches, held) is worth 16 ETH
- The bank issues 224M, burns 122M (55%), ends with 2,981 ETH of permanent liquidity and 1,608 ETH of hard reserves after 718 ETH of buybacks
- $18.1M launch FDV (731 ETH in the pool) → $243M at month 12 (13x)

𝟯 ) 𝗠𝗼𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲:

Assumptions:

450 whitelist seats at 0.15
550 public clearing at 1.00
Team adds 400, 95% into the pool

= 967 ETH in the pool = $23.9M FDV = $0.024 per token.

The system, 12 months out

Assumptions:

- 80% of weeks in expansion
- Traders net buy 5.5% of the pool per expansion week and net sell 3% per contraction week
- 3 year issuance runway, multiplier starts at 1.5x
- All 100 daily licenses clear at 40 days of yield
- 1% of balances retired weekly, 20% of withdrawals sold

That would mean:

- $STANDARD ends at $3.21 (135x launch price and $3.2B FDV)
- Branches hit the 10,000 cap (one branch goes from $29 a day to $264)
- A passive whitelist seat accrues 85K $STANDARD, worth 111 ETH, 738x the cost basis
- A built seat is worth 320 ETH
- The bank issues 367M, burns 191M (52%), ends with 13,823 ETH of permanent liquidity and 13,016 ETH of hard reserves after 2,426 ETH of buybacks
- $23.9M launch FDV (967 ETH in the pool) → $3.2B at month 12 (135x)
