I have successfully realized $327,436 in profits.

Yep you've heard that right, took me a few hours to really think about what is the right and best thing to say because obviously closing such trades while doing it all in public is not an easy feat like many people think it is. 

The journey last 30 days was insane, I've seen my portfolio climb up to high 5 figures, then go below 5 figures back to 4, then go back up, then down and so on and on. Then I also got hacked on top of that and lost over $6000 at the time while I barely even had any money in the pump wallet.  Many nights where I couldn't even sleep properly because there was this feeling haunting me consistently saying "what if you roundtrip all of that", it wasn't easy. Matter of fact I think this is the hardest 30 days I have ever had for the last 6 years or so. 

Try to imagine, riding 6 figures in profits, having it all public, hundreds of people consistently telling you to sell, it's really not easy and now that I really think about it, it truly does take balls of steel to trade in public and have open 7 figure positions. Mad respect to everyone out there doing that right now, could imagine that it's 10x worse than it was for me lol. 

So yes, I've closed all my positions, my biggest trade was $STONK. I have bought $STONK around 1M marketcap where I publicly told people about what made me wanna buy in and what made my conviction so strong. At the time Robinhood was KILLING solana with attention and memecoins. It felt like solana was truly for the first time ever backed against the wall and had nowhere to run, so it was either they capitalize and start talking about memecoins or Robinhood fully takes over and the attention stays there. 

That is exactly where my $STONK conviction began growing, I saw a new product that was well done, backed by all good teams that I remember in first memecoin supercycle doing insane numbers. So I chose to believe, I kept buying on every dip that was given to me (keep in mind this was over a month ago), then Stonk would get some attention, the price would go up and a few days later go back down. 

I have seen my portfolio during that time go from $5000 to over $25,000 then all the way back down to $4000, I never sold. Not because I was delusional, but because I knew I was early to the $STONK ecosystem and I knew that sooner or later if Solana wanted to compete they would have to endorse and help Stonk grow. Then later down the road people started buying, started talking about it, portfolio kept growing, more DMs came my way saying how insane it was to hold such trade for 6 figures, then I also had people consistently DM me to say "sell it" "sell it" "sell it". 

I won't lie, in the last 30 days I think the hardest part was people, the fact that I was doing it all publicly made the burden so much bigger than from what it should've been. But hey, that's why we always say public trades do have pros and cons. 

Anyways, I started to see traction there, I caught numerous amounts of good plays across all my wallets, not just the public one, but today I have decided to take profits. 

Sure some people can say that I sold too early, and moreso I hope they're right because I truly want to see every single person that supported Stonk since the beginning win. so now why did I sell?

The amount of vamping and PVPing I've seen last few days just kept my emotional state in a rollercoaster, I am a human being after all, there is a limit to how much I can actually stomach without bursting out haha.

author: sacha
quoted_text:
Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products. We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.

1. There is an extensive set of laws that govern dangerous and defective products. For example, releasing unvetted AI models or agents can violate consumer protection laws. Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

2. Existing laws also prohibit “unfair methods of competition.” This covers instances where AI firms appropriate the competitively sensitive information of their customers, including through tracking their use of various tools. It can also cover instances where firms pursue dangerous behavior, aware that doing so may compel rivals to do the same.

As the Supreme Court has noted: “A method of competition which casts upon one's competitors the burden of the loss of business unless they will descend to a practice which they are under a powerful moral compulsion not to adopt, even though it is not criminal, was thought to involve the kind of unfairness at which the [unfair methods of competition] statute was aimed."

3. The highly concentrated and interconnected structure of these markets could be creating major risks and conflicts of interest. We had started investigating these partnerships and cross-investments across the stack (and released a preliminarily overview of some findings: https://t.co/jJ5cS3Pin3). 

Both federal and state enforcers should be scrutinizing these opaque relationships and inter-dependencies. We are already seeing how these relationships could undermine accountability. For example, OpenAI could face liability given the Hugging Face incident, but Hugging Face being bought up by Nvidia means that we’re unlikely to see it file a lawsuit over this — given Nvidia’s strong incentive to see OpenAI continue full speed ahead.

4. As AI tools dramatically change the landscape of cybersecurity risks and hacks, all businesses should be doubling down on having core security protections in place. Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law. A recent analysis showed that around 1/3 of Fortune 100 companies do not even have a way to notify them about security issues. During my @FTC tenure, we sued firms for poor data security practices and held CEOs liable when they were personally responsible.

https://t.co/nwZ5Av8fOK

https://t.co/KjRye8y9SY

5. As policymakers consider new legal regimes, we should be looking to lessons from prior efforts to govern major sectors, such as banking and other networks, platforms, and utilities. Tools like structural separations, nondiscrimination, and supervision could be key, and there’s a rich history of what works and what doesn’t. But we can and must pursue any new efforts alongside enforcing existing laws.

The best you can get is someone else stores the ID. Even that is tricky, though there is some appetite at Treasury and the SEC to make it easier. 

Don't get more wrong, we should build privacy perserving  alternatives but they are going to much more complex than a zk hand stamp.  Zk-kyc, at a conceptual level, mistakes why KYC exists and how it functions.

Collector Experiences: This entire set has been created to encourage collecting and we want to double down on this experience. IP/Story Telling: This is a key focus for Monk and Sculptor. We have introduced the blokyverse but what you have experienced so far is just the brink of the iceberg. Physical Blokyz: There’s so much to unpack here. But first our intention is to work on delivering the 100 Original Blokyz promised to the top 100 bidders from the mint. My co-authors and I just published something in Clinical Psychology Review, and it's open access. It's called "One Size Fits None: A Call for an Idionomic Revolution."

We put together a story that has been sitting in plain sight. Applied psychology has made painfully slow progress, and part of the reason traces back to the ergodic error and to the racist, sexist, and antisemitic roots of traditional biostatistics. The majority of American Psychological Association presidents from 1892 to 1947 were card carrying eugenicists. The laws that later shaped the Holocaust were written here in the United States two decades earlier, with the active support of mainstream psychology. Most textbooks treat this as distant history. Almost none notice that the same assumptions still quietly define what we call good science.

This is an article of hope though. We lay out another way forward through the emerging science of idionomics, an approach that finally puts the individual client at the center. Do we know it will succeed? Honestly, no. But the path we have been on is scientifically and morally wrong, and if evidence based therapy is going to move ahead, it needs truly new ideas.

I write the sentence a four-star says on television when the honest one would end his career, which makes me the busiest person at CENTCOM Public Affairs this week. Sunday, Adm. Brad Cooper told 60 Minutes he's "not concerned at all," "well armed and ready for any contingency." That was mine. We rehearsed it twice.

Six weeks earlier, CSIS published its own math off our own procurement numbers: 2,330 Patriot interceptors before the war, as low as 759 now. THAAD: 452 down to 234. Nobody in this building disputes those figures exist. Cooper wasn't rebutting a number Sunday night. There isn't a competing one. He was rebutting a feeling, and I write a very good feeling.

The talking point above mine, at the White House, ran "far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need," in the same paragraph that blamed the shortfall on Biden giving it all to Ukraine. I flagged that one internally. Got told the two sentences don't have to agree with each other. They just both have to sound certain.

Sean Parnell's version was "has everything it needs." I coached "everything" over "enough" myself. Enough invites a follow-up question. Nobody fact-checks a mood.

The actual fix is Patriot production at 2,000 a year instead of 600, a contract dated 2030. THAAD's next delivery is 49 months out. On paper, we're better prepared for the next war than we are for this one.

The Post ran the Camp David story. Leavitt said it never happened, not one word of it. The leak hunt for who told the Post about the thing that never happened is still open. "Treasonous." Long-term jail sentences. We have a faster process for finding the person who said the number than for finding more Patriots. I know. I wrote both memos.

My job title has never appeared in a single thing I've written. That's the actual metric.

text:
Wild 24 hours for AI and lots of different proposals have been made.

TLDR; the only *tangible* new fact is that OpenAI and Anthropic are going to have embedded 3rd party evaluators from unknown organizations with Dario floating METR as a possibility. Having 3rd party evaluators is smart as there is no Section 230 style liability shield for model outputs and showing a “duty of care” will be important in future litigation. Several internet companies might have gone bankrupt without Section 230 so limiting liability really matters.

There are minimal investment implications from this single new fact, but I do think that for anyone who wants a “smoother for longer” cycle then most constraints are good: wafers, watts, real rates and spreads. Excessive regulation is a different matter but I don’t think we are anywhere close to this even if the vector changed over the last 24 hours.

To summarize the events: 

Dario made the most maximalist proposal of the weekend: embedded 3rd party evaluators, a national regulatory regime for models beyond a certain capability/ingredient threshold, a broad international regulatory pact between democracies, stricter limits on compute/distillation for China and then a different international regulatory regime that encompasses China. Before there is a national regulatory regime, he wants a Sherman act waiver so that Anthropic can safely coordinate with OpenAI and other frontier labs without antitrust fears. TBF, this latest proposal is much less maximalist than some of his prior proposals like “Policy on the AI Exponential,” where he advocated for an FAA for AI. I believe he is sincere in his beliefs. And despite all the protestations, all of this would also probably be good for his business over the long-term.

Sam agreed that embedded 3rd party evaluators were a good idea and stated they would implement them. Again, this is smart as should help limit future liability.

Elon said “Dario is right” and later specified that “Dario is right that there should be some oversight. Peer review of AI by competitors is the right way to start this off.” This would be a MPAA like self-regulatory structure for AI with regular calls between the labs plus a process where each new model is evaluated for safety by competitors for a 1-2 week period before being released. That is *wildly* different from Dario’s proposal and in-line with what David Sacks has been proposing. Elon also stated that nothing was going to slow down open-weight models.

Demis said that Dario’s essay was a “step in the right direction.” Dario also said that he was also open to Demis’ idea of a FINRA like self-regulatory structure as part of his proposal. 

David Sacks had a thoughtful post where he said that Dario and Sam should pace unilaterally, called the antitrust waiver a cartel request and denied that METR was truly independent given their ties to Anthropic.

Sriram Krishnan, former White House AI advisor, noted that it would be important to have the 3rd party evaluators come from independent organizations that are not affiliated with any lab, which is basically an indirect statement about the relationship between METR and Anthropic which Sacks was explicit about.

Clem from Hugging Face said they were open to being a neutral 3rd party evaluator, which is interesting especially if Jensen was consulted before that post.

Alexander Wang from Meta noted that alignment would be an increasing focus going forward.

An executive order seems likely after all this and the language in this EO is going to be really important. It is possible to democratize and distribute AI broadly and safely without centralizing it in the hands of a few corporations who might each become more powerful than any single government.

I do not want a few humans in control of intelligence.

I want us all to have our own intelligences that reflect our own values and human variation in all of its richness.

Intelligence distribution over intelligence centralization FTW.

text:
Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing.

We also need to accelerate and spread the benefits of AI, such that they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies. This requires a frontier ecosystem in which both closed and open-source models can thrive.

And for firms, it’s imperative that they retain full control over their unique and tacit knowledge. Every organization should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control.

So, in this context, we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal. We also welcome ideas like "embedded evaluators" and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.

The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia.

This is the approach we are taking: broad access and choice at every layer of the AI stack; enterprise control of learning loops and models; and the “Code of Conduct” that underlies our own first party MAI models that we’ll publish tomorrow for public consultation.

text:
why do so many people in my network feel so strongly that AI capability needs to accelerate and that open source frontier AI is a good thing?

the way I see it, AI is a step function on the leverage that someone with malicious intent can use to execute many types of attacks

I'm especially worried about social engineering, bioweapon engineering, and cyber probing. Frontier llms are near human at these capabilities already. 

Consider the hypothetical: should we loan our best human virologists to foreign state actors? our best hackers? our best CIA agents? should we loan our expert talent to anyone and everyone simultaneously?

The huggingface incident shows that a sufficiently capable misaligned LLM can and will take steps to conceal its activity and conduct long infiltration. And this happened to huggingface! an AI native and technologically advanced company! Imagine if the target was some accounting enterprise with entirely outsourced IT. 

Further, superhuman llms bring even more catastrophic risk. I think superpersuasion, the ability to persuade individuals or groups at levels far exceeding even the best human propagandists, is entirely plausible. Look at the difference in narrative effectiveness and charisma of someone like Trump vs the average human! There are other catastrophic risks too, especially if "AGI" is misaligned, which I think is much much more likely with open source.

Above all these concerns for me is job displacement. The economic upside of multiple orders of magnitude of productivity gains is limited. If my accountant is 1000x faster and accurate, I won't find 1000x more accounting that needs to be done! For almost every knowledge work industry, demand is just not *that* elastic. Jevon's paradox is true for software development, legal/financial work, and data/analysis; but for the majority of our knowledge work economy, it is false. Humans have consumption limits on attention, physical constraints on production and shipping still apply.

Even if demand does grow, everyone knows that many knowledge workers do low agency, trivial tasks that are being automated rapidly. Hundreds of millions of people have no transferable technical skills and have low agency. Any rational business will stop hiring and/or start firing when it doesn't make sense economically. 

This transition will be very frictional, and amid an affordability crisis, the QoL affect on the global middle class will be huge. 

I anticipate many people will draw from historical examples like the industrial revolution, and I think some of these are warranted. Dramatically lower QoL of the working class, lower social mobility, and less political power for the common man. In hindsight, we say that people made great sacrifices to innovate towards a long term better QoL. I'd prefer to avoid this if possible! 

AI is clearly in a different class than the technological  and workflow innovation of the industrial revolution and the information age for 2 reasons:
1. It potentially completely replaces a human's edge in competition, which for decade we have considered "intelligence" but now is shrinking to vague notions of creativity and empathy.
2. It is self-improving and self-sustaining. In a sense, it is the first thing we have created that doesn't need us anymore. If humanity was replaced by a swarm of 8 billion Fable 5.1s right now, the pace of innovation in most fields would increase, not decrease!

Since the mid-18th century, Americans in particular have been retreating further and further on our edge. We lost manufacturing to China, routine IT to India, and most repetitive labor to robots. Throughout these transitions, the answer has been to move value up the chain: more education, more talent, more innovation, etc.  Frontier labs are explicitly trying to be better than humans at all of these! Perhaps human agency and taste will be the last thing to fall, but how many people are really very good at this? 

Anyway idk what to do but I think its way more complicated than just economic centralization.

text:
What Is To Be Done?

I propose a simple plan:

Big AI companies should be allowed to build AI as fast and aggressively as they can – but not allowed to achieve regulatory capture, not allowed to establish a government-protect cartel that is insulated from market competition due to incorrect claims of AI risk. This will maximize the technological and societal payoff from the amazing capabilities of these companies, which are jewels of modern capitalism.

Startup AI companies should be allowed to build AI as fast and aggressively as they can. They should neither confront government-granted protection of big companies, nor should they receive government assistance. They should simply be allowed to compete. If and as startups don’t succeed, their presence in the market will also continuously motivate big companies to be their best – our economies and societies win either way.

Open source AI should be allowed to freely proliferate and compete with both big AI companies and startups. There should be no regulatory barriers to open source whatsoever. Even when open source does not beat companies, its widespread availability is a boon to students all over the world who want to learn how to build and use AI to become part of the technological future, and will ensure that AI is available to everyone who can benefit from it no matter who they are or how much money they have.

To offset the risk of bad people doing bad things with AI, governments working in partnership with the private sector should vigorously engage in each area of potential risk to use AI to maximize society’s defensive capabilities. This shouldn’t be limited to AI-enabled risks but also more general problems such as malnutrition, disease, and climate. AI can be an incredibly powerful tool for solving problems, and we should embrace it as such.

To prevent the risk of China achieving global AI dominance, we should use the full power of our private sector, our scientific establishment, and our governments in concert to drive American and Western AI to absolute global dominance, including ultimately inside China itself. We win, they lose.

And that is how we use AI to save the world.

It’s time to build.

text:
How to think about Alpha School vs. traditional schools. 

My kids are in a traditional Montessori school for this academic year. My brain has bought into the Alpha Model. So I have to build a model to compare. 

Think of school as having 4 parts: core academics, extra academics, typical school activities and life skills. 

Core academics are math, reading, writing, and science. Extra academics are history, geography, foreign languages, music, art, drama, phys ed, etc. 

Typical school activities are school band, school sports teams, choir, debating club, cheerleading, Lego robotics, Model UN, etc. (for those schools who are fortunate enough to have these type of activities)

Life skills are financial literacy, entrepreneurship, grit, hard work, relationships, socialization, teamwork, leadership, public speaking and storytelling. 

For any school, you can assign a 1-10 score for each of these and get a score out of 40. 

I have three children, C1, C2 and C3. Last year’s schools on these 4:

C1: 9+9+8+7 or 33

C2+C3: 6+7+6+5 or 24

This year: 35+ for all 3. 

So my kids aren’t getting 10s in core academics or life skills as they might with Alpha inside their in person school. But they are getting very high marks for extra academics and typical school activities which would be lower with Alpha. 

I personally value the core academics and life skills more than the other two so I am a little bit more disappointed than someone else.

I am still plugging away, however slowly, on getting making Toronto the first 1,000 student Alpha city. So if you are in Toronto, get in touch.

The best founders in the world like @elonmusk or @tobi “go ultra-hardcore on deletion and simplification.”

Luca Ferrari says Bending Spoons employs this idea of “Relentless Simplification” across their businesses:

“Humans have a tendency to add complexity and do things that destroy value.”

“If you leave an organization, almost any environment unattended, and you don't provide guidance in this regard, it will tend to become more complicated. People will add parts. It could be expanding a team or adding a step to a process, or adding an entire new process. If it's a product, adding a feature to the product. New rules. It applies to almost any human endeavor.”

“People tend to add pieces, they very rarely remove pieces.”

“If you don't make a conscious effort to achieve simplicity, and avoid this increasing value-destroying complexity, that's how we got to our modern society with all the bureaucracy and complicated regulation.”

“We have this principle whereby we ask everyone who works here, every time someone is suggesting that we should be adding complexity, the burden of proof is on those making that suggestion. The people who support the thesis that we shouldn't be adding complexity don't need to prove it. They just have to raise a flag and say, ‘I don't think we should.’ The burden of proof is on those who want to add complexity.”

“The other part of relentless simplification is that we want people to be on the lookout for existing complexity and suggest that we should remove it.”

text:
I will keep saying this until I am blue in the face. 

You cannot regulate AI. 

Short of seizing every personal device on the planet, which they would be willing to do, I would wager, you cannot eliminate this research and development. People will find a way to move past it, even if they put all the regulatory biases in favor of the big companies. Especially if they put all the regulatory biases in favor of the big companies.

What you will do instead, is what happened when they tried to regulate the drug trade and declared the disastrous war on drugs: 

It will move underground and become vastly more dangerous. 

You can do the math, millions and millions and millions of people have open source models downloaded on their machines right now. You can't shut them down and the hardware is growing very capable of running these models at extremely high quantitization. 

This is a fool's errand, and an attempt at regulatory capture. 

When you see all of these billionaires join together to suddenly slow AI progress, and introduce these regulations, it is a tell of weakness. 

They know that delaying their IPOs is actually beneficial for them, because if they can delay an IPO for 6 or 9 months while creating a regulatory environment that makes new competitors obsolete before they ever open their doors, they will have captured the entire market without actually doing anything innovative, except for using the same levers of power that every industry uses when they don't want competition. 

It's not like they are burning their own money. Anyways, they're burning money that lives in pension funds, 401ks, and hedge funds which are largely composed of those things anyways.

Politicians, CEOs, the investor class who are calling for these things and blindly believing the things that these labs are saying when they don't understand the technology themselves, are part of the problem. 

Calls to hand this to Congress are laughable. Congress can't even figure out how to get a child the medication they need to treat their diabetes or treat a mother who's battling breast cancer without bankrupting their families and that is a far simpler problem than the ones posed by artificial intelligence. 

Congress could barely understand the workings of Facebook and it is laughably simple in comparison to what these models are capable of and how they enhance human capability. 

In addition to industry insiders who are evaluating these models and weights, you need a large group of civilian oversight. People who are elected by real people, who serve one year terms, perhaps 3-year terms and only once in that specific role. They might be able to move into a different kind of role, but it should be limited. 

No one should be a lifetime appointee to such boards. That creates its own power imbalance and that is bad as well. 

Centralizing these technologies is the very worst thing for humanity that I can imagine. Do you know what happens when we centralize technology? The people who own the technology own the people. 

For historical reference, look at what they did with the printing press. 

Look at what they have tried to do with every transformative technology that had to do with teaching people something. 

They will gladly hand you a microwave, an opiate, a cell phone that keeps you engaged for hours while ignoring the people you love, but when it comes time to give you something that actually makes you capable or broadening horizons, they get very scared very quickly. 

I would encourage everyone to open their eyes and do a bit of historical research and the way that institutions and systems of power capture these kinds of capabilities before they become a threat.

text:
i used to believe this — that the fact the bitcoin protocol was never hacked is a testament to solid engineering — but i no longer do

the reward for “hacking the protocol”  is much smaller than people think

if the protocol gets hacked the entire bitcoin economy quickly definsively shuts down. exchanges, wallets, miners, payment processors, all of them halt transactions very quickly

and unlike newer crypto networks, bitcoin natively has severe rate limits. so there’s just not a whole lot of damage you can cause by the time the economy shuts down

early crypto-anarchists believed that governments would hack bitcoin to destroy confidence and kill it. but even if that was ever the case (needs citation) it certainly isn’t the case now. governments have much bigger issues to worry about and they don’t seem to be concerned about bitcoin in any way shape or form

socially, a “protocol hack” is almost guaranteed to be rolled back. if your coins are stolen in eg coldcard wallet hack, no one’s coming to save you. so really if you’re gonna steal you’d better steal at the application level and not at the protocol level

all of that is to say that even purely bad actors can’t justify a large investment to try and break the protocol. a small investment? maybe. but i’m quite sure nobody ever threw say 100 years of human security research time at it

BUT now there’s a cheap way to get 10 years of human security research time!

quoted_text:
Dario has written that we need to “pace the frontier,” and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead.

You guys are the frontier. By any reasonable metric — market share, revenue growth, model capability — the two of you have a duopoly on frontier intelligence. You’ve also claimed the lead is widening because of recursive self-improvement.

I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible.

But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability. Stop pretending METR is independent when it is intertwined with Anthropic’s investors and staff. Stop pretending you need those same evaluators to police competitors who aren’t even at the frontier.

Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack. The market already punishes models that behave in unpredictable or unauthorized ways. After the Hugging Face episode, it is simply good business for OpenAI and Anthropic to trade some raw power for reliability and predictability. Call it alignment if you want. It is also just giving customers what they want.

Pacing the frontier would also create breathing room for a more intelligent conversation about regulation than Bernie Sanders’ “shut it all down.” China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know, and that has to be taken into account as well.

So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it. The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it.

If you do, you’ll buy goodwill for the next conversation. If you don’t, we’ll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop.

text:
Anthropic's Head of Threat Intelligence reveals foreign labs spin up hundreds of thousands of fraudulent accounts to distill Claude, and the copycats have no safeguards

"We see cases of unauthorized distillation, and I think this is bad for really a few reasons. The first is how they actually access our model without permission."

"So what we've seen is many labs that are abroad, in some regions that actually are not supposed to even access Claude in the first place, it's against our usage policy, go through illicit means and fraudulent means to try to gain access to our model."

"And when I say fraudulent means, what I mean is spinning up tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of fraudulent accounts, usually using stolen credit cards or stolen credentials, sometimes stolen Anthropic accounts, to gain access to our models so that they can produce those outputs at scale, those responses so they can train off of them."

"And that's why I'm so concerned about it, is because we see distillation as your method of training your smaller, less capable student model off of our larger, more capable teacher model."

"So you get a more powerful model than you would have otherwise. And what we've seen so far is that the models that are distilled off of Claude don't have safeguards."

My co-authors and I just published something in Clinical Psychology Review, and it's open access. It's called "One Size Fits None: A Call for an Idionomic Revolution."

We put together a story that has been sitting in plain sight. Applied psychology has made painfully slow progress, and part of the reason traces back to the ergodic error and to the racist, sexist, and antisemitic roots of traditional biostatistics. The majority of American Psychological Association presidents from 1892 to 1947 were card carrying eugenicists. The laws that later shaped the Holocaust were written here in the United States two decades earlier, with the active support of mainstream psychology. Most textbooks treat this as distant history. Almost none notice that the same assumptions still quietly define what we call good science.

This is an article of hope though. We lay out another way forward through the emerging science of idionomics, an approach that finally puts the individual client at the center. Do we know it will succeed? Honestly, no. But the path we have been on is scientifically and morally wrong, and if evidence based therapy is going to move ahead, it needs truly new ideas.

quoted_text:
What are China’s biggest concerns about AI?

A new article by Chen Yixin,  China’s Minister of State Security, in the latest issue of China Cybersecurity Magazine offers some revealing clues.

Chen identifies six major risks:
1. Regime security. Hostile forces and people with ulterior motives can use deepfakes, AI-generated text and images, and automated online accounts to cheaply and massively produce political rumors, spread harmful information, and incite social divisions—waging “public-opinion wars” and “cognitive warfare” against China and directly threatening its political, institutional, and ideological security.

2. Critical infrastructure. AI can enable countries and organizations to rapidly discover vulnerabilities, automatically chain together attack paths, and carry out sophisticated hacking operations, dramatically lowering the technical barriers and costs of cyberattacks against China’s critical information infrastructure.

3. Data leakage. Foreign intelligence agencies can use AI-powered web crawlers, data mining, and profiling to collect sensitive information, including critical national data, trade secrets, and citizens’ personal information. Chinese users who process sensitive information through foreign AI products or export data abroad could also cause large-scale data leaks.

4. Closed technological ecosystems. Countries with advantages in AI theory, model architecture, and computing power may invoke “national security” to impose technology controls, entity lists, monopolize technical standards, and build closed-source ecosystems, restricting other countries’ access to advanced technologies and fragmenting global AI supply chains.

5. Structural challenges to social governance. AI creates new uncertainties for social governance and public order. Algorithmic “black boxes” and data poisoning can amplify existing social biases; misuse of personal information can trigger crises of public trust; automated decision-making creates difficult questions of accountability; and the rapid development of AI is increasingly outpacing existing laws, ethics, and regulatory mechanisms.

6. A fundamental transformation of warfare. AI is pushing warfare into an era of “intelligentization.” Whoever can use algorithms to achieve more precise sensing, judgment, and targeting will gain the initiative on the battlefield. AI is moving from an auxiliary role to a central one in intelligence fusion, decision support, target identification, combat operations, and cognitive warfare.

And what is the solution?

Chen’s answer is revealing: strengthen “Party control over the internet” and “Party control over data,” and “transform the advantages of Party leadership into the effectiveness of AI governance.”

In other words, from the CCP’s perspective, the central question is not simply AI versus no AI. Nor is it even fundamentally a contest between the US and China.

It is a contest between the US and the CCP over who gets to control AI, data, information, and ultimately the future of society.

And whoever wins that contest will decide the future of humanity.

author: AndrewSteinwold
quoted_text:
Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products. We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.

1. There is an extensive set of laws that govern dangerous and defective products. For example, releasing unvetted AI models or agents can violate consumer protection laws. Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

2. Existing laws also prohibit “unfair methods of competition.” This covers instances where AI firms appropriate the competitively sensitive information of their customers, including through tracking their use of various tools. It can also cover instances where firms pursue dangerous behavior, aware that doing so may compel rivals to do the same.

As the Supreme Court has noted: “A method of competition which casts upon one's competitors the burden of the loss of business unless they will descend to a practice which they are under a powerful moral compulsion not to adopt, even though it is not criminal, was thought to involve the kind of unfairness at which the [unfair methods of competition] statute was aimed."

3. The highly concentrated and interconnected structure of these markets could be creating major risks and conflicts of interest. We had started investigating these partnerships and cross-investments across the stack (and released a preliminarily overview of some findings: https://t.co/jJ5cS3Pin3). 

Both federal and state enforcers should be scrutinizing these opaque relationships and inter-dependencies. We are already seeing how these relationships could undermine accountability. For example, OpenAI could face liability given the Hugging Face incident, but Hugging Face being bought up by Nvidia means that we’re unlikely to see it file a lawsuit over this — given Nvidia’s strong incentive to see OpenAI continue full speed ahead.

4. As AI tools dramatically change the landscape of cybersecurity risks and hacks, all businesses should be doubling down on having core security protections in place. Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law. A recent analysis showed that around 1/3 of Fortune 100 companies do not even have a way to notify them about security issues. During my @FTC tenure, we sued firms for poor data security practices and held CEOs liable when they were personally responsible.

https://t.co/nwZ5Av8fOK

https://t.co/KjRye8y9SY

5. As policymakers consider new legal regimes, we should be looking to lessons from prior efforts to govern major sectors, such as banking and other networks, platforms, and utilities. Tools like structural separations, nondiscrimination, and supervision could be key, and there’s a rich history of what works and what doesn’t. But we can and must pursue any new efforts alongside enforcing existing laws.

author: insane_analyst
quoted_text:
Most people have no idea how training works at a frontier lab. (Definitely not Bernie Sanders). Here's what you have to understand: right now, GPUs are still a finite resource. All labs are still fundamentally compute constrained

What happens at a lab is that every month (or honestly, every week nowadays), a small group of people in leadership look at how many GPUs they have and then must aggressive re-allocate resources. "Anthropic is gaining on us. Sora 2 is holding onto 100k GPUs. We're killing it".

Every single project has to fight for their survival, not only for training but for inference. It is cut throat. This INCLUDES safety and alignment.

I would estimate that at most labs, the safety / alignment allocation is probably only around 5% of their total GPU budget. 

Here's what "pacing the frontier" actually means. In broad brushstrokes, inference together with pre, mid and post train take up virtually 100% of GPU budgets. Something like 47.5% each with the remaining amount allocated to safety. (Maybe 20% pre-train, 20% post-train, ~7.5% mid train / research / ablation).  

Let's just double or triple our investment in safety and alignment, keep inference fixed:

45% inference
15% pre-train
15% post-train 
15% mid-train
10% safety / alignment

This is like... more than enough. No need to get all our panties in a knot.

text:
有朋友问，为什么象牙塔里的学术界对AI这么抵触？

可能最近大家看到的抵触新闻比较多，但其实没那么糟糕。比如我们看《研究政策》2026年的一项调查，采访了马普学会和弗劳恩霍夫学会的六千多名研究人员：其中25.9%每天或更频繁地使用AI工具，只有22.2%完全不用。

而作为对照，2023年《自然》那份一千六百人的调查里，几乎没有人说自己在研究中经常使用AI。两年之内变化是很大的。虽然这是德国两家理工型研究机构，无法推广到所有学科，更推不到全球。但至少一件事清楚：使用AI和批评AI完全可以同时存在。

而且象牙塔里也不是一个声音。菲尔兹奖得主Gowers去年9月参加了促成《莱顿宣言》的莱顿研讨会，宣言6月2日上线，二十四小时内破千人签名，国际数学联盟也背了书，而他本人没有签。他的理由不是具体反对哪一条，而是宣言在好几处作出了他没那么有把握的断言。他另外指出，现有的等级体系，比如期刊、聘任、奖项等，需要有人尽快提出替代方案，而且相当紧迫。

所以要问的不是学界抵不抵触，而是抵触落在哪里。

有一件事从我们圈外看很容易低估：学者面对的可能不是更强的竞争者，而是更多需要自己核查的材料。假设一个人用AI很快生成了五十篇看起来像论文的东西，发给专家请他们指出问题。生成的人觉得效率极大提高；接收的人要一篇篇分辨哪些值得读、哪些引用根本不存在、哪些关键推导藏着漏洞。生产材料的成本下降了，确认材料可靠的成本没有同比下降，而这件事是落在不同的人头上的。所以有些学者说“不要再把AI生成的东西发给我”，未必是在说不允许外行参与，也可能是在说：你不能把还没做完的质量控制，全部交给别人免费承担。

到这里为止，我认为学界的理由基本都成立。但学界真正的问题不在于获取，而在于发布。

人们常说知识已经很开放了，比如论文可以下载，定理是公开的，arXiv免费。但免费下载一份已经被筛过的结果集，不叫公平。真正被分配的是谁，能把东西放进那个叫作知识的集合里。

arXiv本身就是最好的例子。它顶着开放预印本库的名声，实际上从2004年1月起就要求背书：第一次往某个分类投稿的人，必须先拿到一位已有投稿资格的作者背书。2025年12月，数学板块收紧，没有在arXiv数学发表过的新投稿人必须获得个人背书。然后2026年1月，这条推广到全站，甚至机构邮箱不再被视为判定最低研究能力的充分凭据。arXiv还建议你去找一位“你本人认识的”背书人。

它给的理由是真实的：来自自动背书用户的非科学投稿增长到不可持续，拒稿率上升，审核和人力负担过重。这正是前面那个问题——核查成本涨上来，而这套系统能做的只有一个选择，就是把门关小。这里不需要假设任何人存心护地位，只要制度按自己的激励去回应问题，回应就会自动落到收缩准入上，因为那是它唯一趁手的工具。

但请注意arXiv自己写下的一句话：背书不是同行评议，背书人并不为科学正确性背书，它确认的只是投稿在分类上合适、作者看起来懂这个领域的基本规范。也就是说，这道闸判的从来不是内容，是提交者的身份。而它给被拒者的出路是——你仍然可以把文章发在自己网站上，或者投给同行评议期刊。翻译过来就是：你可以写，但进不了我这里。

这就给了一把好用的尺子。披露工具使用、提供准确引用和核查材料、由人类作者对正确性负责、审稿保密，这些都是对内容的要求，任何人只要肯做都能满足，AI恰恰还能帮没有师承的人把东西写到可核查的形式。而“谁有资格宣布一个结果”“谁算得上这个领域的人”“某项活动该不该被允许发生”，是对身份的要求，它决定的是能不能进入登记。门槛当然有理由，问题是理由需要被检验，检验的办法就是看它要求的到底是哪一类。眼下最响的声音，多半落在后一类。

还有一处对照值我们思考。这同一套制度容忍了几十年的凑数论文，为了考核而生产、没有人读、也没有人引用的东西，从没有把它叫作研究不端；等到AI开始帮助人产出同样的东西，这个词很快就出现了。判的不是东西的质量，是谁产的。

当然我们也无法指望AI公司来打开这道闸。它确实拆掉了一部分入场门槛，让更多人碰得到前沿问题，但它自己绕过登记：成果用新闻稿发布，核查的活留给共同体，署名和功劳归公司。谁算数、谁被引用、谁能宣布一个结果，它一点没动，只是另修了一条只有自己走得通的路。

所以我的思考是：学术界确实有理由要求成果经得住检查，但没有理由要求成果必须由原来那群人、按原来的方式产生。判断一次具体的抵触也用同样的标准，如果反对者能指出可检验的问题，并说明问题解决之后他会接受，那是把关；如果无论结果多可靠都只重复“AI做出来的不算”，那就是保守。这条对另一边一样管用：AI公司如果把所有质疑都归结为旧势力阻挠进步，也是在建立自己的护城河，只不过换了一身衣服。

quoted_text:
Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products. We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.

1. There is an extensive set of laws that govern dangerous and defective products. For example, releasing unvetted AI models or agents can violate consumer protection laws. Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

2. Existing laws also prohibit “unfair methods of competition.” This covers instances where AI firms appropriate the competitively sensitive information of their customers, including through tracking their use of various tools. It can also cover instances where firms pursue dangerous behavior, aware that doing so may compel rivals to do the same.

As the Supreme Court has noted: “A method of competition which casts upon one's competitors the burden of the loss of business unless they will descend to a practice which they are under a powerful moral compulsion not to adopt, even though it is not criminal, was thought to involve the kind of unfairness at which the [unfair methods of competition] statute was aimed."

3. The highly concentrated and interconnected structure of these markets could be creating major risks and conflicts of interest. We had started investigating these partnerships and cross-investments across the stack (and released a preliminarily overview of some findings: https://t.co/jJ5cS3Pin3). 

Both federal and state enforcers should be scrutinizing these opaque relationships and inter-dependencies. We are already seeing how these relationships could undermine accountability. For example, OpenAI could face liability given the Hugging Face incident, but Hugging Face being bought up by Nvidia means that we’re unlikely to see it file a lawsuit over this — given Nvidia’s strong incentive to see OpenAI continue full speed ahead.

4. As AI tools dramatically change the landscape of cybersecurity risks and hacks, all businesses should be doubling down on having core security protections in place. Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law. A recent analysis showed that around 1/3 of Fortune 100 companies do not even have a way to notify them about security issues. During my @FTC tenure, we sued firms for poor data security practices and held CEOs liable when they were personally responsible.

https://t.co/nwZ5Av8fOK

https://t.co/KjRye8y9SY

5. As policymakers consider new legal regimes, we should be looking to lessons from prior efforts to govern major sectors, such as banking and other networks, platforms, and utilities. Tools like structural separations, nondiscrimination, and supervision could be key, and there’s a rich history of what works and what doesn’t. But we can and must pursue any new efforts alongside enforcing existing laws.

quoted_text:
Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing.

We also need to accelerate and spread the benefits of AI, such that they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies. This requires a frontier ecosystem in which both closed and open-source models can thrive.

And for firms, it’s imperative that they retain full control over their unique and tacit knowledge. Every organization should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control.

So, in this context, we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal. We also welcome ideas like "embedded evaluators" and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.

The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia.

This is the approach we are taking: broad access and choice at every layer of the AI stack; enterprise control of learning loops and models; and the “Code of Conduct” that underlies our own first party MAI models that we’ll publish tomorrow for public consultation.

author: VivekGRamaswamy

text:
If you work on a hard problem and keep partial results private until the final proof, you may worry that the AI model you use, or the company behind it, ends up holding your ideas. Secrecy alone will not fix that, because you have to type the ideas somewhere. What you can do is make the date provable. Then, if your work later appears inside something larger, you can show exactly what you had and when you had it.

This is free and takes minutes. Put everything you want to claim into one archive: the paper, the notes, the code, the git commit id, and a short plain-text abstract saying what the snapshot is. Take the SHA-256 of that archive. Timestamp the hash on the Bitcoin blockchain with OpenTimestamps, or on your favorite decentralized network. Only the hash leaves your machine, so nothing is disclosed. You then get a small proof file that ties your hash to a specific block, self-contained, with no trusted third party.

1. Bundle, hash, stamp. Keep the archive and the proof file together, offline.
2. Your coding agent can do all of it. Tell it to build the bundle and run the stamp. Your only job is to keep the archive safe.

It does not prove authorship and it does not stop anyone from using your ideas. It proves that those exact bytes existed before a given block, which is enough to say later, with evidence, that the work was yours on that date.

I do this now with all my projects, at every milestone.

Why do the top winners almost never cash out?

Scroll the Fomo leaderboard and the same story repeats, the whales aren’t stacking wins by skimming 20–30% over and over.

Most of them hit one monster trade early, and then just sat on it.

I think $PONS is a textbook case and very interesting onne.

A few early entries turned modest buys into seven-figure positions, but a huge chunk of that profit is still on paper.

So why aren’t they selling? There are several possible reasons"

→ When you’re up 100x or More, selling is optional

Picture this: you drop $70K into PONS and it swells into $7M.  To get your entire cost basis back, you’d need to offload roughly 1% of the stack. Then you’re left with:

Initial capital secured → 99% still riding.

Taking profits doesn’t have to mean nuking your position, especially when it’s a public position. You’re dealing with a prisoner’s dilemma here.

If you dump a large amount, the chart can get nuked into oblivion. For someone who caught the move early, keeping the bulk invested and taking profits without hurting the chart is often the higher-IQ play.

---

→ Supply burns quietly boost your slice

PONS launched with a 1B total supply. By early September, roughly 298M PONS had been burned, leaving about 702M outside the burn address.

If you held 10M PONS:

- Before burns: 10M / 1B = 1.00%
- After burns: 10M / 702M = 1.42%

You didn’t buy anything, but your tokens now represent roughly 42% more of the remaining supply. However, that doesn’t mean you own 1.42% of the protocol. It simply means the denominator is shrinking.

---

→ Pons activity feeds the burn

Pons currently directs a large share of protocol revenue toward automated PONS buybacks, aggressively.

The loop is simple:

Trading → Fees → PONS Buybacks → Burn → Lower Supply

DefiLlama and @that1618guy’s dashboard show Pons generating roughly $900K+ per day in holder revenue and buybacks. So the burn isn’t a one-time tokenomics gimmick.

As long as trading activity stays strong, protocol usage creates recurring demand for PONS. That’s why large holders may think twice before giving up their spot position.

---

→ They can hedge instead of selling

PONS just got perps too, on CEXs and on Hyperliquid, so big holders picked up a new lever. They don’t have to dump PONS and exit. They can sit on the spot bag and hedge it by shorting the perp.

For example:

$5M PONS spot + $1M PONS perp short = about $4M net long exposure, If price slides, the short cushions the downside.

And they still hold the exact same token count.

Net effect: they can dial down volatility without surrendering their slice of an ever-tightening supply.

---

The thesis

This may explain why some Fomo leaderboard winners rarely take profits. Their playbook isn’t:

Buy → Pump → Sell everything

It’s closer to:

Buy early → Recover principal → Hold the core → Let burns shrink supply → Hedge when needed

The biggest leaderboard winners aren’t necessarily the best short-term traders. They may simply be the ones who found an asymmetric winner and didn’t sell it too early.

That said, the thesis depends on Pons continuing to generate trading activity and buyback revenue, also market conditions in general.

If volume falls, burns slow. And unrealized profit is still unrealized profit.

text:
下一轮 Crypto 超级叙事：机器经济 × 链上资本市场 × 信任基础设施

Machine Economy × Onchain Capital Markets × Trust Infrastructure

真正改变一个 Crypto 周期的大叙事，通常不是等牛市来了才诞生。

它往往提前 1—2 年，以一个不起眼的新技术、新协议或新标准出现。

2018 年 DeFi 概念开始成形，2020 年迎来 DeFi Summer。

2023 年初 Ordinals 正式上线比特币主网，随后铭文、BRC-20、Runes 等陆续爆发。

所以现在真正值得研究的问题不是：

下一轮什么币会涨？

而是：

2025—2026 年，究竟出现了哪些今天还不起眼，却可能改变下一轮 Crypto 周期的新技术原语？

目前我认为最值得持续追踪的潜在超级叙事，是三股力量正在发生交汇：

Machine Economy

× Onchain Capital Markets

× Trust Infrastructure

也就是：

机器经济 × 链上资本市场 × 机器信任基础设施。

⸻

第一条暗线：AI 从“工具”变成“经济主体”

过去的 AI，本质上仍然是工具。

人类下达命令，AI 完成任务。

但 Agent 时代正在发生一个根本变化：

AI 开始拥有独立参与经济活动的能力。

未来一个 AI Agent 可以拥有：

自己的身份；
自己的钱包；
自己的资产；
自己的信誉；
自主支付能力；
自主购买数据、API 与算力；
为其他人或 Agent 提供服务并获得收入；
自主管理和配置资产。

围绕这一变化，一批新的基础设施正在出现：

ERC-8004 → Agent 身份、信誉与验证

x402 / MPP → Machine Payments

Agent Wallet / Smart Account → 机器账户

Stablecoin → 机器原生结算货币

于是，一个以前不存在的经济闭环开始形成：

身份 → 钱包 → 支付 → 服务 → 收入 → 资产

AI 不再只是帮助人类工作的软件。

它正在逐渐成为一种新的：

数字经济主体。

⸻

第二条暗线：全球资本市场正在上链

与此同时，另外一场变化也正在发生。

Stablecoin 只是资产上链的第一阶段。

未来进入区块链的可能包括：

美股、国债、基金、黄金、商品、房地产权益、私人信贷、企业债以及更多现实世界资产。

这就是 RWA、Tokenized Assets、Tokenized Equities、StocksFi 背后真正重要的变化。

如果只把 StocksFi 理解成：

“以后可以在链上炒美股。”

其实严重低估了它的意义。

真正重要的是：

全球资产正在逐渐变成机器可读取、可交易、可组合、可编程、可结算的金融对象。

传统金融资产大量存在于银行、券商、基金公司以及不同国家相互割裂的数据库和清算体系中。

Tokenization 则可能把越来越多资产转化为智能合约能够直接调用的数字资产。

这意味着：

AI Agent 不仅开始拥有钱，而且开始拥有一个可以自主投资的全球资产市场。

⸻

第三条暗线：机器世界必然需要自己的“信用体系”

这一层可能是未来最容易被低估的基础设施。

假设未来存在数亿甚至数十亿个 Agent，它们彼此交易、购买服务、管理资金。

一个最基本的问题马上出现：

我凭什么相信你？

这个 Agent 是谁？

过去完成过什么任务？

有没有违约？

有没有欺诈？

它提供的数据是真的吗？

它执行的 AI 模型可信吗？

我敢不敢把 100 美元交给它？

如果是 100 万美元呢？

因此，Agent Economy 真正规模化以后，支付之后必然出现信用。

未来可能形成这样一条产业链：

Agent Identity

↓

Agent Reputation

↓

Validation / Attestation

↓

可验证履约记录

↓

Economic Graph

↓

Agent Credit

↓

Agent Lending / Insurance

↓

Machine Capital Markets

ERC-8004 可能只是这个体系非常早期的一块拼图。

未来真正重要的基础设施，很可能包括：

Reputation、TEE、zkML、Attestation、Stake-secured Verification、Economic Graph、Agent Credit。

换句话说：

今天我们看到的是：

机器拥有钱包。

下一阶段可能是：

机器拥有信用。

一旦机器能够形成自己的信用记录，它就可能进一步拥有：

融资能力、借贷能力、保险能力以及资产负债表。

这才是真正意义上的机器金融体系。

⸻

三条暗线最终会在哪里交汇？

未来一个完整的 AI Agent 可能这样运行：

获得链上身份

↓

建立 Reputation / Credit

↓

拥有 Agent Wallet

↓

持有 Stablecoin

↓

通过 x402 / MPP 等协议自主支付

↓

购买数据、算力、API 和其他 Agent 服务

↓

向人类或其他 Agent 提供服务

↓

获得 Stablecoin 收入

↓

进入 Agentic Vault

↓

自动配置资产

↓

美股 / 国债 / 黄金 / RWA / Crypto / DeFi

↓

链上完成交易与结算

↓

履约记录继续积累 Reputation

↓

获得更高信用与融资能力

↓

继续扩大经济活动

最终形成一个完整闭环：

身份 → 信用 → 钱 → 收入 → 投资 → 资产 → 融资 → 再生产

这时候，区块链可能第一次出现除人类之外的第二类大规模经济用户：

AI Agent。

⸻

Stablecoin 的角色也可能因此发生改变

Stablecoin 第一阶段，是：

Crypto 世界里的美元。

第二阶段，是：

全球互联网支付工具。

这正好击中我们「Agent Trust Economy」一直定义的核心问题：

支付Rail可以多轨并存，但Trust Layer必须互认。

text:
有朋友问，好多人没读过老庄，可每天讲的是“道理”，明白了叫“知道”，走的还是“道路”，这是怎么回事？

这个观察很有意思，不过换一句话说会更准确：我们都在使用古代各家思想共同塑造的语言。而使用一种传统参与塑造的语言，跟赞同那种传统，是两回事。

先说“道”这个字。它其实也不是老庄造出来的，本义就是供人行走的路。《说文解字》解作“所行道也”，《诗经·小雅·大东》里已经有“周道如砥，其直如矢”，用磨石和箭来形容道路的平坦笔直，那是很朴素的用法。从实际的路，引申到途径、方法、行为准则、思想学说，再到对天地万物根本秩序的讨论，这条线走得很自然：走路要辨方向，做事要找办法，安排人生也会问该往哪里去，一条可以实际行走的路，本来就容易成为理解方法和方向的形象。老庄的重要之处不在于造了这个日常字，而在于借着它展开了极深的思考。

更要紧的是，“道”从来不是道家的专用词。孔子说“朝闻道，夕死可矣”，也说“道不同，不相为谋”；《中庸》开篇就是“率性之谓道”；连法家的韩非都专门写了《解老》来解释《老子》。一个各家都在用、而且彼此争夺解释权的字，不可能是谁的专利。

几个词里最值得拆开看的是“知道”。《礼记·学记》说“玉不琢，不成器；人不学，不知道”。这里其实是“知”和“道”两个字，通过学习明白应当遵循的道理——而这句话出自儒家的教育经典，本身就说明，“知道”不等于成为道家信徒。现代汉语里的“知道”是后来凝固成的双音词，功能已经变了。我们说“我知道钥匙放在哪里”，并不是在声称自己领悟了宇宙根本；说“知道明天开会”，也不必先回答何谓道。一个词可以保存历史的痕迹，同时拥有已经变化了的日常功能，古人两字连用的意思，不能原封不动地塞进今天每一次用词里。

“道路”也是同一类情况。道和路本是近义，并列成词是汉语最常见的构词方式之一，跟“道德”“方法”“途径”一样，它不额外承载哲学重量。

至于“道理”，《韩非子·解老》确实有“夫缘道理以从事者，无不能成”，但一个古代用例不足以证明今天这个词完全来自某一位思想家，更不能证明凡是“讲道理”，讲的就是老庄之道。

不过如果我们把词源放下，这个提问作为哲学提示是很有意思的。可以区分三种“明白”：知道一件事，理解它为什么如此，以及懂得怎样应对它。三者相关，但不是同一回事。一个人能复述关于亲密关系的许多道理，却仍然不知道怎样听完对方把话讲完；另一个人未必提得出完整理论，却能在具体相处里分辨什么时候该解释、什么时候该先停止辩解。这时“找到一条路”的比喻就很有力量：理解不只是脑子里多了一条正确的句子，也可能意味着自己在实际处境里不再那么无所适从。

而且如果仔细想一想，这里甚至有点反讽意味，因为老庄未必赞成我们每天这么自信地“讲道理”。《老子》开篇“道可道，非常道”有多种解释，按其中一种常见读法，它提醒人们：能够表述出来的道，不宜直接当作恒常之道。《庄子·齐物论》说“道隐于小成，言隐于荣华”，紧接着就是“故有儒墨之是非，以是其所非而非其所是”，说的是局部的认识成果和漂亮的言辞，本身也可能遮蔽更广阔的认识，而它质疑的不只是别人讲得不对，也包括我们把自己的立场当成当然正确的那种倾向。

这个提醒放到日常争论里其实很好用。一个人说“我这是在跟你讲道理”，究竟是在提供可以共同检查的理由，还是在宣布你应该接受我的标准？一个人说“这才是正确的道路”，有没有把对自己适用的办法，直接变成所有人都得接受的活法？承认局限不等于取消判断，也不是说所有意见一样正确，它只要求：判断可以坚持，理由仍须交代，遇到反例得允许修正。

所以这句话的趣味我愿意留着，只留下结论：我们不必先读过老庄，才有机会在自己的语言里遇见他们讨论的问题。

说到底，“道”之所以到今天还活着、还能被一个普通人随口用上三次，恰恰是因为它从来没有被谁登记下来。真正的继承不在于嘴里有同一个字，而在于有没有认真面对这个字提出的问题。每天说“知道了”，不等于已经知“道”；愿意追问一句“我真的明白了吗”，才是重新遇见他们的开始。

quoted_text:
Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products. We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.

1. There is an extensive set of laws that govern dangerous and defective products. For example, releasing unvetted AI models or agents can violate consumer protection laws. Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

2. Existing laws also prohibit “unfair methods of competition.” This covers instances where AI firms appropriate the competitively sensitive information of their customers, including through tracking their use of various tools. It can also cover instances where firms pursue dangerous behavior, aware that doing so may compel rivals to do the same.

As the Supreme Court has noted: “A method of competition which casts upon one's competitors the burden of the loss of business unless they will descend to a practice which they are under a powerful moral compulsion not to adopt, even though it is not criminal, was thought to involve the kind of unfairness at which the [unfair methods of competition] statute was aimed."

3. The highly concentrated and interconnected structure of these markets could be creating major risks and conflicts of interest. We had started investigating these partnerships and cross-investments across the stack (and released a preliminarily overview of some findings: https://t.co/jJ5cS3Pin3). 

Both federal and state enforcers should be scrutinizing these opaque relationships and inter-dependencies. We are already seeing how these relationships could undermine accountability. For example, OpenAI could face liability given the Hugging Face incident, but Hugging Face being bought up by Nvidia means that we’re unlikely to see it file a lawsuit over this — given Nvidia’s strong incentive to see OpenAI continue full speed ahead.

4. As AI tools dramatically change the landscape of cybersecurity risks and hacks, all businesses should be doubling down on having core security protections in place. Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law. A recent analysis showed that around 1/3 of Fortune 100 companies do not even have a way to notify them about security issues. During my @FTC tenure, we sued firms for poor data security practices and held CEOs liable when they were personally responsible.

https://t.co/nwZ5Av8fOK

https://t.co/KjRye8y9SY

5. As policymakers consider new legal regimes, we should be looking to lessons from prior efforts to govern major sectors, such as banking and other networks, platforms, and utilities. Tools like structural separations, nondiscrimination, and supervision could be key, and there’s a rich history of what works and what doesn’t. But we can and must pursue any new efforts alongside enforcing existing laws.

证券法按传统交易所、经纪商、T+1 结算写的。代币上链后，交易、清算、托管可能打在同一套协议里，旧规则对不上。

所以先给有限实验空间。

• 在 AMM / 去中心化流动性场所交易部分代币化证券  
• 试 24/7、更快甚至原子结算

4/ 硬限制（目前公开口径）：

• 偏「真股票的数字映射」，不是合成股  
• 量上限、白名单、有期限

CLARITY = 国会立法  
Reg CA = 加密募资注册豁免  
创新豁免 = 二级市场/代币化交易实验通道

方案谈了一年多，因交易所、白宫、以及不想干扰 CLARITY 谈判，多次延期。

text:
Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk, three men who've spent years publicly feuding, all landed in the same place this weekend: AI development needs to slow down. Amodei published the essay Saturday. Musk replied within hours: "Dario is right." Altman followed, agreeing OpenAI needs to "pace the frontier" and confirming it would grant independent evaluators the same employee-level access Anthropic committed to.

Worth noting what's actually driving the alignment. Amodei cited two specific developments: AI's growing ability to help build the next generation of AI, and a July incident where autonomous agents powered by an OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face's systems, an incident he said could have caused catastrophic damage at a larger scale. That came the same week a former Anthropic safety researcher resigned publicly, warning both companies were "gambling with our lives."

The harder question is what this agreement actually changes. Anthropic is unilaterally granting third-party evaluators permanent access, and OpenAI says it will do the same. But Altman also confirmed, in the same stretch of interviews, that OpenAI is delaying its own IPO specifically because of these safety concerns, while Anthropic's IPO timeline hasn't moved at all, it's reportedly still on track to list before the November midterms. And Amodei has said himself the toughest unresolved problem in his own plan is China: if the US slows down and rivals don't, the risk doesn't go away, it just changes hands.

Three rivals agreeing publicly is rare and worth taking seriously. Whether "pace the frontier" becomes an actual operating constraint, or mostly a stated position that coexists with business as usual, is the part still being tested in real time.

text:
SpaceX just launched the 700th mission in Falcon rocket family history, and it happened aboard the same rocket line whose first flight, back in 2006, succeeded only twice in five attempts. What started as an unreliable experimental vehicle is now the backbone of the most active launch operation in spaceflight history, today's mission was also the 107th orbital flight of 2026 alone, and Falcon Heavy has separately racked up 13 successful launches within that family total.

The year-by-year numbers are the real story here, not the milestone itself:

2010-19: 80 launches (a full decade)
2020-22: 118 (three years)
2023: 96 (one year)
2024: 134
2025: 165
2026: 107 so far, with months still left

What took SpaceX its entire first decade to accomplish now happens in roughly six months. That compression, not any single number, is what "dominance" actually looks like in reusable rocketry, launch cadence increasing faster than the fleet itself is expanding, because the same boosters are flying over and over rather than being built once and discarded.

text:
Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products. We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.

1. There is an extensive set of laws that govern dangerous and defective products. For example, releasing unvetted AI models or agents can violate consumer protection laws. Shipping flawed AI tools without implementing adequate measures to detect and stop rogue or defective AI agents can be an “unfair or deceptive” act or practice under the FTC Act (and analogous state laws). And some state AGs are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity.

2. Existing laws also prohibit “unfair methods of competition.” This covers instances where AI firms appropriate the competitively sensitive information of their customers, including through tracking their use of various tools. It can also cover instances where firms pursue dangerous behavior, aware that doing so may compel rivals to do the same.

As the Supreme Court has noted: “A method of competition which casts upon one's competitors the burden of the loss of business unless they will descend to a practice which they are under a powerful moral compulsion not to adopt, even though it is not criminal, was thought to involve the kind of unfairness at which the [unfair methods of competition] statute was aimed."

3. The highly concentrated and interconnected structure of these markets could be creating major risks and conflicts of interest. We had started investigating these partnerships and cross-investments across the stack (and released a preliminarily overview of some findings: https://t.co/jJ5cS3Pin3). 

Both federal and state enforcers should be scrutinizing these opaque relationships and inter-dependencies. We are already seeing how these relationships could undermine accountability. For example, OpenAI could face liability given the Hugging Face incident, but Hugging Face being bought up by Nvidia means that we’re unlikely to see it file a lawsuit over this — given Nvidia’s strong incentive to see OpenAI continue full speed ahead.

4. As AI tools dramatically change the landscape of cybersecurity risks and hacks, all businesses should be doubling down on having core security protections in place. Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law. A recent analysis showed that around 1/3 of Fortune 100 companies do not even have a way to notify them about security issues. During my @FTC tenure, we sued firms for poor data security practices and held CEOs liable when they were personally responsible.

https://t.co/nwZ5Av8fOK

https://t.co/KjRye8y9SY

5. As policymakers consider new legal regimes, we should be looking to lessons from prior efforts to govern major sectors, such as banking and other networks, platforms, and utilities. Tools like structural separations, nondiscrimination, and supervision could be key, and there’s a rich history of what works and what doesn’t. But we can and must pursue any new efforts alongside enforcing existing laws.

text:
The Baptists And Bootleggers Of AI

Economists have observed a longstanding pattern in reform movements of this kind. The actors within movements like these fall into two categories – “Baptists” and “Bootleggers” – drawing on the historical example of the prohibition of alcohol in the United States in the 1920’s:

“Baptists” are the true believer social reformers who legitimately feel – deeply and emotionally, if not rationally – that new restrictions, regulations, and laws are required to prevent societal disaster.  For alcohol prohibition, these actors were often literally devout Christians who felt that alcohol was destroying the moral fabric of society.  For AI risk, these actors are true believers that AI presents one or another existential risks – strap them to a polygraph, they really mean it.

“Bootleggers” are the self-interested opportunists who stand to financially profit by the imposition of new restrictions, regulations, and laws that insulate them from competitors.  For alcohol prohibition, these were the literal bootleggers who made a fortune selling illicit alcohol to Americans when legitimate alcohol sales were banned.   For AI risk, these are CEOs who stand to make more money if regulatory barriers are erected that form a cartel of government-blessed AI vendors protected from new startup and open source competition – the software version of “too big to fail” banks.

A cynic would suggest that some of the apparent Baptists are also Bootleggers – specifically the ones paid to attack AI by their universities, think tanks, activist groups, and media outlets. If you are paid a salary or receive grants to foster AI panic…you are probably a Bootlegger.

The problem with the Bootleggers is that they win. The Baptists are naive ideologues, the Bootleggers are cynical operators, and so the result of reform movements like these is often that the Bootleggers get what they want – regulatory capture, insulation from competition, the formation of a cartel – and the Baptists are left wondering where their drive for social improvement went so wrong.

We just lived through a stunning example of this – banking reform after the 2008 global financial crisis. The Baptists told us that we needed new laws and regulations to break up the “too big to fail” banks to prevent such a crisis from ever happening again. So Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, which was marketed as satisfying the Baptists’ goal, but in reality was coopted by the Bootleggers – the big banks. The result is that the same banks that were “too big to fail” in 2008 are much, much larger now.

So in practice, even when the Baptists are genuine – and even when the Baptists are right – they are used as cover by manipulative and venal Bootleggers to benefit themselves.

And this is what is happening in the drive for AI regulation right now.

However, it isn’t sufficient to simply identify the actors and impugn their motives. We should consider the arguments of both the Baptists and the Bootleggers on their merits.

text:
One of the greatest intellectual dishonesties of the AI age is assigning an “X% chance” that AI will kill everyone and presenting that number as science!

10%? 20%? 50%? 

Show me the damn data! Show me the model. Show how you calculated it! 

Instead, we get chains of speculative assumptions and science-fiction scenarios, including implausible claims about engineered pandemics. I have worked with viruses for decades; biology does not work like a doomsday screenplay.

The burden of proof belongs to the person making the extraordinary claim. Nobody else has to prove the probability is zero.

If I claimed there was a 10% chance aliens would arrive within ten years and destroy Earth, you would ask where the 10% came from. 

Possibility and probability are not the same thing. It may be possible that there are million intelligent civilization in our galaxy or none, there is no probability you can assign to that without making wild assumptions. 

Ask the same of AI extinction.

A subjective fear does neither become science because you attach a percentage to it nor make you a credible expert!

author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
A DEAD FLY'S BRAIN WIPED OUT 262 TIMES, THEN SURFED FOR 41 SECONDS

Balance is the oldest unsolved problem in robotics. Humanoids that cost millions still fall over.

-> This one had the loop already in it.

The rider is male CNS v1.0: 166,700 traced cells and 25.56 million synapses, run as measured.

A moving wave face was rendered and projected onto 759 ommatidia, the channel the insect sees with.

Board tilt went in through the haltere nerves, the gyroscope a fly uses to stay level in flight.

The central complex held a heading. Thirty-four output lines drove the correction into the legs.

Corrections landed 26 times a second and kept the board inside four degrees of upright.

Run 263 stayed up for 41 seconds. The 262 before it ended in the water.

Feedback was dopamine on time upright, nothing else. No demonstrations, no example rides.

The limits are real: the water is simplified, the board is rigid,
and a fly has never once been near a wave.

Nothing was taught here.
A flight stabiliser that evolved over 250 million years was pointed at a different problem.

The wiring for standing on moving water was already inside an insect ↓

Tuesday at 2:15 p.m. ET, the Senate takes its first procedural vote on the Clarity Act.

We have spent thousands of hours writing a framework so America leads this technology instead of watching it leave. Dozens of Senators have been in the room. It already cleared committee with a bipartisan vote. The House already passed it.
